during the tour.  
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
3.      The Chairman informed that the agenda of the meeting was to hear the Secretary, Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping & Waterways on the subject ‘Functioning of Major Ports in the Country’. The 
Chairman remarked that it had been seven years since the launch of Sagarmala, the flagship 
programme of the Ministry,  and desired to know the progress made in Port Modernization and 
Connectivity, Port Led Industrialization, Operational Efficiency and Ease of Doing Business at 
Major Ports and the challenges still existing in these areas. He further desired that the Secretary 
may brief the Committee on the following points: 
i. Landlord Port model of governance and its anticipated impact on the autonomy and 
functioning of Major Ports; 
ii. Status and progress of the upcoming 13th port - Wadhawan in Maharashtra;  
iii. Development of Transshipment hubs at Indian ports; 
iv. Financial performance of Major Ports; 
v. Details of the number of PPP projects undertaken at each Major Port; 
vi. New legislations or amendments to existing legislations proposed to improve the 
functioning of the ports; 
vii. Details of ‘Green Ports Policy’ and the targets set to establish green/sustainable ports; 

129 
 
viii. Steps taken to create SMART ports, implementation of the Port Community System 
(PCS) paperless regime and digitization at Major Ports; and 
ix. Policy guidelines on land management at ports, the status of the ‘One Time Settlement 
Scheme’ and the success of the dispute settlement institution mechanism, ‘SAROD-
PORTS’. 
4.         The Committee was infor med about the legislative framework governing the Major and 
Non-Major ports wherein Major Ports feature in the Union List and are generally governed by 
Ministries. Non-Major Ports feature in the Concurrent List and come under State Governments 
and are gove rned either by State Maritime Boards or directly by the State Government.  The 
Major Port Authority Act, 2021  is applicable to all the Major Ports and contains provisions for 
their constitution, administration, control, and management while  the Indian Ports  Act, 1908 is 
applicable to both Major and Non -Major Ports and contains provisions related to the notification 
of ports, pilotage and other operations.   
5. The Committee was informed that there are total 225 ports on the approximately 7,517 
km Indian coastline out of which, 12 are Major Ports and 213 are Non-Major Ports.  Both east 
and west coasts have 6 Major Ports each ; Kolkata, Paradip, Visakhapatnam, Kamarajar, Chennai 
& V.O. Chidambaranar on the east coast and   Cochin, New Mangalore, Mormugao, Mumbai, 
JNPA & Deendayal on the west coast. The total traffic cargo handled by all the ports, both Major 
and Non-Major in 2022-23 was 1445 Million Tonnes (MT) out of which 795 MT was handled by 
Major Ports and 650 MT by Non-Major ports. The capacity utilization was 49% and 64% for 
Major and Non-Major Ports respectively. 
6. The Secretary, MoPS&W informed the Committee that the Major Ports have achieved 
historic all-time high performance of improvement in terms of cargo handling and significant 
improvements in several other parameters. The total traffic cargo handled by all the ports, both 
Major and Non-Major, in 2022-23 is 1,445 MT of which 795 MT is the share of Major Ports and 
650 MT is the share of Non-Major Ports. The earlier trend where Non-Major Ports had greater 
share in cargo handling has been revised after much effort. The Committee was also apprised 
about the following achievements and improvements in the FY 2022-23: 
 Highest Ever Total Cargo handled by Major Ports – 795 Million Tonnes; 
 Total Capacity of Ports -2627 Million Tonnes per Annum (1617 MTPA for Major Ports 
and 1010 MTPA for Non-Major Ports);  
 Best Ever Vessel Turn Around Time – 52 Hours; 

130 
 
 Highest Ever Output per Ship Berth Day – 17239 Tonnes; 
 Best Ever Operating Ratio – 48.54 %; 
 Highest Container Throughput at JNPA – More than 6 million TEUs; 
 Highest Ever Vessels handled – 21846; 
 9 PPP projects worth Rs. 9,544 crores awarded; and 
 Operating Surplus, i.e. the difference between Operating income and expenditure, is 
about Rs. 9,365 crores. 
7. The Ministry informed the Committee that the above figures are the averages for all 12 
ports. The Paradip Port has exceeded 30,000 tonnes per day in Cargo Volume and Jawaharlal 
Nehru Port (JNPA) has achieved a Turnaround time of 24.8 hours, comparable with the global  
best ports like Shanghai and Singapore. 
8. The Ministry further informed that a number of initiatives are being taken by the Major 
Ports to move towards Sustainable Development Goals and to decarbonize the operations at the 
ports in line with the Maritime In dia Vision 2030 and the Panchamrit Commitments made in the 
UN Climate Change Conference in Glasgow (COP -26). The Ministry highlighted the following 
green initiatives taken by the Major Ports :- 
 Wind and Solar Energy installations at Major ports for increasing the share of renewable 
energy ; 
 Port Vessels/ Vehicles’ /Equipment retro-fitted with electrically powered equipment in 
transition to Green Fuel; 
 Shore to Ship Power Supply to reduce carbon footprint of ports ;  
 Port activities like bunkering, handling and storage facilities for low carbon fuels under 
the National Green Hydrogen Mission; and 
 Other Initiatives-Use of Energy Efficient Products i.e. LED Lamps, BLDC Fans and 5 
Star Air Conditioners. The Committee was also informed that the Ministry was due t o 
launch "Harit Sagar" guidelines for Green ports in a few days' time to ensure the 
achievement of the Maritime India Vision for 60% green renewable energy use by Major 
Ports by 2030. 
9.         The Committee was also informed of the initiatives taken by the Ministry for developing 
digital tools and dashboards for real -time data exchange to promote Ease of Doing Business.   
The Committee was apprised about ‘Sagarmanthan’ - a digital dashb oard to monitor both the 
operational and financial performance of  ports, used by the Ministry for weekly reviews and the 

131 
 
‘National Logistic Portal’ (NLP Marine) for maritime stakeholders - a single integrated digital 
window to access information on various  regulatory bodies, shipping line, port/terminal 
operators and services such as cargo, banking financial, etc. 
10.       The Ministry also informed that to provide more autonomy to ports, the Tariff Authority 
for Major Ports (TAMP) has been abolished and t ariffs are now fixed based on the market 
dynamics. The Model Concession Agreements have been realigned with the market requirements 
to benefit both cargo and port owners.  
11.       Some Members pointed out that the presentation did not have data regarding international 
ports for comparison with the performance parameters of Indian ports.  The Chairman directed

12.       A Member remarked that all the Major ports were constructed m ore than 50 years back 
but till date not more than 45 -50% of their capacity has been utilised. He enquired about the 
reasons for such non -utilisation of capacities. The Secretary responded that in the port sector, 
capacity utilisation of 70 per cent is con sidered to be saturation. In the last eight years the 
capacity of ports has increased from 872 MT to 1600 MT. A 50% utilisation means that there is 
additional capacity to handle more cargo and without such addition, the ports would be 
congested. 
13.       Upon enquiry by a Member on the development of new ports, the Secretary informed that 
a new Port at Vadhavan, about 150 kms north of Mumbai is being developed.  Environmental 
Impact Assessment studies have all been done except one and the Dahanu Taluka Envi ronmental 
Protection Agency has to do public hearings and give its NOC. JNPA is the nodal agency 
developing the Vadhavan port.  The new port would be a deep draft port with 18 -20 metres of 
draft which would enable even the largest capsize vessels to come to the port.

Transshipment Hub in Greater Nicobar Island called Galathea Bay. Environmental clearance had

2. The Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and the witnesses who were 
present. The Chairman informed that the agenda of the meeting was to hear the representatives of 
the Indian Ports Association (IPA) and Indian Private Ports and Terminals Associa tion (IPPTA) on 
the subject ‘Functioning of Major Ports in the Country.’ The Chairman asked the representatives of 
IPA and IPPTA to brief the Committee on various aspects of functioning and modernisation of 
ports. 
3. Through his presentation, the Secretary, IPA informed the Committee that the IPA is a 
society of the 12 Major Ports in the country. 
4.  The Committee was informed that in the FY 2022 -23, the Major Ports had a total Operating 
Income of Rs. 18,198 Crores and an Operating Surplus of Rs. 9,365 Crores. H owever, the Net 
Surplus was Rs. 6,993/ - Crores because a lot of the surplus has to be put into the pension fund to 
meet pension liabilities. Due to pension liabilities, three major ports —Mumbai, Mormugao, and 
Cochin—are currently having financial difficult ies. They have also explained various activities 
undertaken by them to improve the profitability of ports. 
5. The Committee was also apprised of the major achievements in the performance of various 
Major Ports in the FY 2022-23. 
6.         The Committee was i nformed about the comparative statistics of the Major Ports and top 
global ports. The Port of Singapore ranks 31 st globally with a draft of 18 Meters, 18 hour TRT and 
37.5 Million Twenty -foot Equivalent Units (MTEU) and Qingdao Port (China) with a draft of  17 
Meters, 40.8 hour TRT and 630 MTEU ranks 42 nd globally while India’s JNPA ranks 54 th with a 
draft of 15 Meters, 22 hour TRT and 6 million plus MTEU. However, due to its impressive 
turnaround time (TAT) of just 22 hours (equal to 0.9 days) JNPA has jump ed nine places in the 
Overall Performance Index according to the Logistics Performance Index Report, 2023 of the World 
Bank. The total handling capacity of JNPA will get increased to about 10.4 million metric tons 
which will be the maximum the port can han dle. Therefore, JNPA has begun planning for the 
forthcoming port of Vadhavan in Maharashtra, which will have a draft of 18 to 20 meters, 9 berths 
each measuring one kilometer in length and a maximum capacity of around 24.5 million TEUs.  
7.         The Com mittee was informed that the privatization of berths helps in increasing the 
efficiency and productivity of ports.  The Chairman of Paradip Port informed that all berths in 
Paradip Port, the largest cargo handling port on the east coast, are proposed to be  mechanized by 
2030. He also informed that mechanization is the only way to control pollution as the port handles 

137 
 
coal and iron ore which are highly dusty cargos. Upon query by the Chairman regarding the effect of 
mechanization on employees, it was informe d that the Paradip port has a very lean staff with the 
majority of staff employed on contractual basis and after mechanization, the staff will be diversified.  
8.         The Chairman of the Kandla Port informed that the port was the largest in terms of ca rgo 
handling. Massive investment has been made in infrastructure for new roads, godowns, railways, 
and housing.  
9.         The Committee was informed that ‘Harit Sagar’ Green Port Guidelines, 2023  have been 
launched to achieve zero carbon emission goals and to increase India’s share of renewable energy to 
60% by 2030. The Committee was further informed that IPA has launched ‘Sagar Setu,’ a national 
maritime single window platform encompassing complete end -to-end logistics solutions as the 
International Mar itime Organization (IMO) has announced that from 1 st January 2024, it will be 
mandatory for ports around the world to operate Maritime Single Windows  (MSWs) for the 
electronic exchange of information required on ships. 
10.       The Committee was also info rmed that India aims to increase cruise passenger traffic from 
0.4 million at present to 4 million and the economic potential of Cruise tourism is expected to go up 
from USD 110 million at present to USD 5.5 billion in the years to come.  
11.       The Secretary-General of the Indian Private Port and Terminals Association, through written 
and oral submissions, enumerated the various issues faced by the Private operators:- 
 Concession agreements signed between PPP Operators and the Port Authorities are heavil y 
skewed in favour of the Ports due to: 
a. The inefficient and inequitable allocation of risks in PPPs; 
b. Lack of flexibility in contractual arrangements; and 
c. Lack of robust review mechanism keeping in pace with the dynamic changes in trade. 
 Existing Concessionaires should be allowed to migrate to the New Model Concession 
Agreement, 2021, by signing Supplementary Agreements, in order to opt   for the benefits given 
to new Concessionaires like lease rentals, freedom in fixation of Tariffs etc. This would  give a 
level playing field to both the existing and new Concessionaires. Upon a query by the Chairman 
regarding the land lease rentals, the Secretary -General, IPPTA informed that revenue share is 
being paid by the Concessionaires to the Port    Authority which should cover all the expenditure 
from the point of view of the concession. However lease rentals are also being charged 
separately for the old Concessionaires under the Agreements of 2008, 2013 and 2019 while as 
per the new Concession Agreement, land is to be given at a very nominal rate.    

138 
 
 High port charges for mainline ship calls make Indian ports uncompetitive compared to global 
ports.   
 The success of a port depends on proper rail and road connectivity without which port / terminal 
assets are unde rutilized, thus increasing the pre -berthing delay of vessels. Connectivity plans 
should be part of the project scope from the initial stage itself.  
 Additional charges such as Railway Terminal Charges, and Siding Charges collected by Ports 
increase the overall logistics costs. 
 Non-resolution of various disputes between the Port Authorities and the Concessionaires. The 
new Dispute Resolution Mechanism of SAROD -Ports is applicable to new Concessionaires. 
Further, though the Government has set up Conciliation and Settlement Committees , the Ports 
sometimes withhold their consent to refer the disputes to these Committees.  
 Lack of institutional mechanism for providing long-term and liberalised financing.  
 Lack of regulatory measures for preventing unhealthy compe tition between Major Ports and 
Non-Major Ports and integrated planning of development of infrastructure  
 Dredging expenditure is met by the ports themselves which add to the marine related charges. As 
per international practice, dredging expenditure is borne by the Government.

there is a government authority though terminals are private. The Member also asked about the 
advantages and disadvantages of the transition f rom Port Trust to Port Authority, the differences 
between the old and new Concession Agreements and whether any objections had been raised 
regarding the old terms and conditions. The representatives of the IPA informed that some problems 
had not been anticipated at the time of signing of the agreements but due to changes in scenario over 
the years, modifications were sought in the agreements. New model concession agreements were 
announced in 2008 and 2018 and then in 2021. There is an inbuilt review mechani sm in the 
concessionaire agreements. Port authorities are however reluctant to review old agreements.

provisions are inbuilt in every agreement which can be invoked for future changes.

benefit the people and the nation. The representative of the IPPTA opined that in a market-driven 

139 
 
economy, market forces would invariably determine the type of cargo to be handled by the ports, the

16.       Another Member commented that presently, PPP projects are handling about 51 per cent of

 Rated as India’s Most efficient port for the second consecutive year by a World Bank 
agency 
 APMT has a measurable impact on local job creation; it has emplo yed over 2500 people 

143 
 
at the Pipavav port, among which, 90% are Gujarati people from surrounding villages. 
 APMT Pipavav has 2 Container berths with capacity to handle up to 1.35 Million TEUs, 
 a  Dry Bulk  Berth with capacity of 4 Million tonnes of dry bulk  cargo, a Liquid Berth 
with capacity to handle upto 2 Million Tonnes of liquid cargo and a RoRo facility with 
capacity of handling about 2,50,000 cars per year.   The port also has 12 Rail Sidings and 
17 Warehouses.  
 A new liquid berth for INR 720 Crores i s under development at the Port which will 
increase the liquid cargo handling capacity of Port to 5.2 MMT. 
 Utilisation capacity was 55-6-% 
 The port has about 500 regular employees.  
4.        The Committee was apprised about the sustainability initiatives taken by the Port under 
the Gujarat Green Gateway project, namely, conversion of cranes from diesel to electric, 
commissioning of 1000 Kilo Watt rooftop solar power plant inside the port premises reusing 
treated wastewater for plantation of 250,000+ trees and that 40% of energy was sourced from 
green sources.  The target was to make Pipavav a Green Port by 2030.  
5.        The Committee was also informed about the following digital and technological 
advancements achieved by the APMT Pipavav: 
i. Integrated Operations Centres  
ii. Advanced analytics: 
 Predictive maintenance 
 Supply chain planning 
iii. Artificial intelligence: 
 Automated planning, despatching & execution 
iv. Automation: 
 Machine learning approach using digital history 
 Intelligent assets (onboard) 
 Digital Twin 
6.        The representative explained that the focus on technology was very strong to further 
improve productivity.  Digital twin was already operational at one of the Company’s terminals at 
Nhava Sheva, World -class N4 Terminal Operating System and PrimeRo ute had been 
implemented to improve efficiency and reduce the Port Stay Hour of Customer vessels.  
7.        The Committee was informed about the CSR initiatives of the port which cover: 

144 
 
 72+ major water conservation structures (12 check dams, 07 farm ponds , 58 RRWHS, 
pond deepening & desilting); 
 Benefit of port medical facility & ambulance support to over 2000 villagers; 
 Women are trained in nursing, electrical, BPO, LED trade under the Saksham scheme and 
 Providing clean drinking water to villages. 
8.        A Member pointed out that the Port did not appear to have Skilling Programmes for 
industry-specific skills like Crane Operators or Forklift Operators and cited the example of 
Germany where every port had such training.   He suggested that the Port could tie up with the 
National Skill Development Council.  
9.      The Committee was also informed about the challenges faced by the Port, such as, the 
underdeveloped eco-system predominantly agricultural but with good potential for industry, poor 
road connectivity, and uncompetitive rail freight since nearly 65% of the cargo in India moves by 
road and customers are unwilling to shift to rail freight due to the high costs as compared to road 
freight. A Member commented that the cost of road freight per tonn e per kilometre ranged from 
Rs. 3-Rs. 3.5 whereas the freight charges of railways should be less than Rs. 1.   He asked for a 
comparative chart of the basic fare of DFC with roads and railways as the Committee would be 
hearing the DFCCIL soon.  
10.      The Committee was also informed that the grant of subsidy to designated ports for Liquid 
cargo handling is putting other ports in a disadvantageous position; Permits and clearance delays 
and the cessation of benefits of SEIS to exporters are the other problems faced by Private ports.  
11.      The representative of the Pipavav Port further briefed the Committee on the Dedicated 
Freight Corridor remarking that it would be a game changer as  the infrastructure which has been 
created by the Railways is going to gi ve seamless access to the northern hinterland which is the 
main market of the Port and efficiencies that would reduce the transportation costs. A Member 
asked whether the DFC was presently in operation till Pipavav and was informed that the 
Pipavav port was connected by the DFC to Surendranagar and onwards to the mainline through a 
feeder line. Katuwas near Rewari in Haryana was the starting point of the DFC which connects 
the port.  The DFC was presently operational and was already a game changer because trains that 
used to take 72 hours to come to the port now come in 30 hours and are double -stack electrified 
trains.  The Member commented that the DFC was the biggest project in the country and its 
biggest impact would be on changing the logistical costs.  

145 
 
12.      A Member asked about the future plans of the Port as the Concession Period was due to 
expire soon and was informed that the Government of Gujarat was in the process of formulating 
a policy on it. The Member commented that there should be a compara tive chart with figures 
from other ports including top foreign ports regarding the investments in technology, asset 
utilization, efficiency parameters etc.  
13.      Through his presentation, the Sr. Vice -President, of JSW Jaigarh Port  informed the 
Committee that the port at Jaigarh has a cargo handling capacity of 55 MMTPA with 70% 
capacity utilization and is the highest sugar exporter amongst the private ports in India. It has 7 
berths and a dedicated specialised MBC loading facility f or Inland waterway transportation.   
Twenty-five per cent plus of Indian coastal movement is being done from Jaigarh to Dharamtar.   
The Jaigarh Port has a draft of 18.5 meters with infrastructure designed for 20.5 metres and the 
cost of dredging was around 300 Crores. The port can handle Capesize ships and Triple E size 
vessels for Containers with its world -class infrastructure. The CAGR growth of volume handled 
in Jaigarh Port is around 15 per cent year on year 
14.      JSW also operates India’s largest sta te-of-the-art Riverine port Dharamtar in Maharashtra 
situated on the banks of Amba River that has a capacity of 34 MMTPA and draft of 3.5 meters,   
the country’s first Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) based LNG terminal at 
Jaigarh Port  and the single largest coal export facility in India at Paradip. The Jaigarh port has a 
strategic location and serves Central India as well as Andhra Pradesh and Goa.   
15.      The Committee was informed about the digital initiatives and technological advancements 
in the Jaigarh Port: 
 Enhancing Port Community Systems, iPortman management system 
 IoT and Sensor Integration 
 Digital Road Map 
 Integrated Digital Platform  
 IOT and Predictive Maintenance (PM)  
 Metaverse (AR/VR) for operational and Safety training  
 Digital Logistics Management Systems (DLMS)  
 NLP (Marine) System upgradation to reduce logistics costs to 9%, Indian Customs 
Electronic Data Interchange Gateway (ICEGATE) customs interactions and EoDB 
initiatives for stakeholders 
 Smart Gate Automation & WB Aut omation for TAT monitoring,  controlled truck 

146 
 
movements and reducing congestion and TAT/TRT, paperless work etc. 
 Electronic Control on Cargo Delivery for Engineering Control on cargo delivery to 
Group Company, less human intervention and increased productivity 
 System Upgradation - Lock Mobile & Allow Limited Application, Visitor Management 
System, One click report for customer 
 Navigation simulation for training purposes  
16.      The Committee was also informed about the Port’s commitment to sustainable  initiatives 
like covershed operations, dust suppression systems, shore to ship power, LED lights etc.  It was 
however pointed out that the Ministry stipulates that bio -fuel should be bought from a certified 
supplier whereas there are no certified bio-fuel suppliers in the country.  
17.      The Committee was informed that JSW Jaigarh port has 125 regular employees and 1498 
contractual employees while JSW Dharamtar has 97 regular and 451 contractual employees. The 
Port’s CSR initiatives like training girls in the BPO industry, sea -cage fishing etc were 
highlighted. The representatives of both ports informed the Committee that they had their own 
residential colonies with facilities for employees within the townships, all statutory benefits and 
welfare measures and constant training programmes for the employees.  
18.      A Member enquired about the greater number of contractual employees versus the regular 
employees and was informed that this was because the jobs of the port industry workers were 
mostly seasonal in nature. The contractual employees were also given the same benefits as the 
regular ones. Upon enquiry whether CSR funds can be provided beyond the state, it was 
informed that though focus was on surrounding areas, there were no limitations. Upon enqu iry 
by a Member about employment prospects after training,  it was clarified that the girls being 
imparted vocational training under CSR programmes were finding employment outside. The 
Member commented that though the Gujarat Pipavav port had existed for 25 years, there were no 
hospitals or medical facilities for the employees. The representatives opined that running a 
hospital needed help from the local administration; another Member suggested that the Port 
could build a Hospital and get an NGO to run it.  
19.      Regarding the gaps in connectivity, the Committee was informed that the  Jaigarh Port is 
connected to Pune -Bengaluru Highway.  The Mumbai -Goa Highway -66, about 40 kms away 
from Jaigarh port is under construction but Container traffic can be moved o n the Highway only 
if it is 4 lanes.  Both these Highways have parallel railway lines, one being Konkan Railway and 
the other being the Central Railway line from Pune to Bengaluru.   However, there is no rail link 

147 
 
between these two lines which is the bigges t hurdle hampering the full potential of this port.  If 
two sanctioned projects of Railways at Chiplun Karad and Vaibhavwadi Kolhapur or an Inland 
Waterway connection to the Chiplun Industrial Area is given, the port can be developed as a Hub 
and Spoke Model.  
20.      Regarding port -led industrialisation, the  Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate 
Change (MoEFCC) is giving environment clearances for particular cargo with quantity 
restrictions which are not good for Ease of Doing Business. The Shipping industry is not static 
like the Manufacturing industry it always varies with Government p olicies and market 
conditions. Applying for MoEFCC’s consent for cargo change would delay the process by 
almost a year.  The representative suggested that MoEFCC should  revert to its earlier policy of 
giving a blanket 80 million capacity to handle broad cargos.  
21.      Upon enquiry by the Chairman about the tariff policy and suggested changes, the 
representative of the Jaigarh port stated that the Concessionaire Agreement of the Port was with 
the Maharashtra Maritime Board and was for 50 years duration.   He opined that market-driven 
tariff was best for minor ports as this facility has also been provided to major ports, though there 
is a disparity between the older Concessionaires and the new ones. The representative of the 
Gujarat Pipavav port also stated that with in the same port, different tariff regimes are applicable 
to different terminals which creates disparity and opined that all tariff regimes should be market -
based.  
22.      The Chairman asked the representatives to reply to the ten questions handed over t o them 
and the questions raised in the meeting within a week.  
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
23. The Committee decided to take up the following three subjects for examination. 
 Development of niche tourism including spiritual tourism, theme -based tourist ci rcuits 
and potential tourist spots; 
 Development and expansion of existing and new national inland waterways; and 
 Functioning of Archaeological Survey of India. 
24.      The Committee further decided to undertake a study visit to Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh), 
Bengaluru (Karnataka) and Goa from 3 rd to 7 th July 2023 for detailed examination of various 
subjects under consideration and mandate of the Committee  viz., Functioning of Archaeological 
Survey of India with reference to the State of Karnataka; Development of Niche Tourism 
(including Spiritual Tourism), Theme -based Tourist Circuits and Potential Tourist Spots in the 

148 
 
States of Andhra Pradesh & Goa; Development and Expansion of Existing and New National 
Inland Waterways, with reference to the States of Andhra Pradesh & Goa; Construction of Road -
Over-Bridges (ROBs), Road-Under-Bridges (RUBs), Service Roads and Review of Road Survey 
Guidelines etc., with reference to the State of Goa; and Visit to Manohar International Airport, 
Mopa, Goa on Development of the Airport and Facilities available to the passengers. During the 
visit, the Committee will hold elaborate deliberations with various stakeholders and 
representatives of the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Goa and Karnataka on the issues 
related thereto, as per the Tour programme.  The Committee authorized the Chairman of the 
Committee to seek necessary approvals from the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha for the 
purpose.

2. The Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and informed them that the 
agenda of the meeting was to hear the representatives of Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation

the purpose. 
(After the representatives of DFCCIL took their seats) 
4.        The Chairman welcomed the representatives of DFCCIL and stated that the Committee 
had been apprised of the connectivity issues faced by the ports to the hinterland which impedes 
the productivity and performance parameters of the po rts.  He asked DFCCILto brief the 
Committee on  the following:- 
 Last-mile connectivity and the high logistics costs in India 
 The number of seaports in India connected to the Eastern and Western Freight Corridors; 
 Impact of the connectivity provided by DFC on logistics costs; 
 Comparison of the freight charges of DFC with road and rail cargo tariffs; 
 Reasons behind the delay in the implementation of the DFC project which started in 
2006; 

151 
 
 Status of completion of the Eastern and Western Freight Corridors; 
 Cost escalation due to the delay and the details of new Corridors to be undertaken in 
Phase II of the Project; 
 The problems anticipated as regards the shifting/redesignating the entire supply chain 
developed on the road mode to rail mode; and 
 The steps taken to prevent congestion and accidents at both corridors. 
5.        The representatives of DFCCIL, through their presentation, informed the Committee of 
the total length of DFCs in the country, allocation and funding, ports connected to DFCs, DPR 
status of DFC projects, etc. as given in Annexure–II. 
6.  The representatives of DFCCIL informed that Ports like Kandla, Mundra, Pipavav, and 
Hazira have been connected to the DFCs through the feeder routes. 33 Good Sheds (7 in EDFC 
and 26 in WDFC) have also been developed. The Detailed Project Report (DPR) has b een

Palghar-Bhusawal-Dankuni and Rajkharswan-Andal of 2,106 km and Itarasi -Vijayawada of 931 
km, which will provide direct connectivity to ports, namely, Dhamra, Paradip a nd Gopalpur in 
Odisha, Visakhapatnam, Gangavaram and Kakinada in Andhra Pradesh.  
7.  Members enquired about the reason for the non -inclusion of Cochin and Vizhinjam Port 
in the DFC network.  DFCCIL informed that under the National Rail Plan -Vision 2030, the total 
length of future DFC would be 7,800 kilometers by the year 2050, which will cover the 
remaining areas.  
8. Members raised various queries such as: 
 Need for Road Under Bridges/underpass/tunnel facility etc. on DFC for easy movement 
of cattle; 
 Lack of connectivity of Ports in South India to DFCs; 
 Need for a chart depicting freight costs levied by Indian Railways and DFCCIL 
separately; 
 Need for a Feeder route/line connecting North Eastern Region of the country to the 
Stations of Sonnagar-Dankuni of the EDFC;  
 Provision of Wagons to coastal area fishermen of Pipavav and Kandla Ports; 
 Key areas and the responsibilities of DFCCIL as far as employment is concerned; and 
 Profit gained/losses incurred by the DFCCIL in the development of DFCs and the 
challenges faced in this regard.

and took note of the suggestions made by the Members. The Chairman directed that written 
replies to the points which had not been answered and t o the questions forwarded by him may be 
sent within a week. 
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
(After the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism and other officials took their seats) 
10. The Chairman welcomed the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism. He then remarked that 
despite India being a 365 -day tourist destination offering a diverse array of products for Niche 
Tourism as well as various Theme -based Tourist Circuits and diverse geographica l features, the 
tourism potential still remains untapped. He queried about the reasons why India has been unable 
to fully exploit its potential for Niche Tourism as compared to its smaller neighbours, namely, 
Thailand, Nepal, and Bhutan who are achieving t remendous success in becoming the top golf, 
mountain, and sustainable tourism destinations respectively. He further queried about the areas 
identified for the development of Niche Tourism in the country, the number of Niche Tourism 
projects under implement ation, particularly in three important categories of Tourism - Medical, 
MICE, and Spiritual Tourism, challenges faced in developing a destination as a Niche Tourism 
hub and the coordination mechanisms employed by the Ministry with various State 
Governments/ Departments/ agencies. The Chairman asked the Ministry to apprise the 
Committee of the number of projects completed and those which are under development under 
the Theme-based Tourist Circuits identified under the ‘Swadesh Darshan Scheme (SDS) Phase -
1’ along with their physical and financial progress and the time and cost overruns, the status of 
Spiritual Circuit projects and further plans for their development.   He also enquired into the 
reasons for the SDS moving away from Theme -based tourist circuits and focusing on revamping 
Destination Tourism, potential tourist spots identified under the ‘SDS -2.0’ and the criteria 
employed for selection, steps taken for the welfare of local communities and creation of 
employment opportunities in the areas identified for the Scheme. 
11. The Chairman then remarked that many States like Assam, Gujarat, Kerala, Rajasthan, 
Punjab, Goa, Karnataka, Uttarakhand, Maharashtra, Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and 
Tripura have granted 'industry' status to tourism, which provide s benefits such as electricity 
tariff, lower local taxes, availability of land on subsidized rates, etc. But the hotel and resort 
industry being capital-intensive require huge investments and has long gestation periods.   Hence, 
the Ministry should take up the issue with the State/Central Government to grant the hotel and 
resort industry the ‘infrastructure’ status to enable it to avail longer credit terms, greater 
investments, and better access to commercial borrowings as well as tax benefits/concessions. H e 
also queried about the reason for the delay in the implementation of the Draft National Tourism 
Policy which was released in July, 2022.  
12. Through her presentation, the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism informed the Committee 
that the Ministry is current ly promoting ten Niche Tourism Products, namely, Sustainable 

153 
 
Tourism, Rural Tourism, Adventure Tourism, Eco -tourism, Meetings Incentives Conferences & 
Exhibitions (MICE), and Wedding Tourism, Cruise Tourism, Medical & Wellness, Film Tourism 
and Golf Touris m and Spiritual Tourism.   The Ministry informed the Committee of the steps 
taken for each Niche product, viz. formulation of National strategies in consultation with State 
Governments and Industry, guidelines and framework for each Niche tourism product, and 
launch of Travel for LIFE Programme under Sustainable Tourism. The Ministry has also 
launched the Best Tour ism Village Competition to identify the potential areas which received 
751 applications from Rural Tourism Villages.   E-Conference Visa was also granted for the 
MICE events.  Also, the Ministry has launched a new Incredible India film on MICE Tourism

Environment, Forest & Climate Change for   Eco-Tourism, (ii) the Ministry of Shipping, Ports, 
and Waterways, for developing coastal areas/destinations under Cruise Tourism, (iii)   the M/o 
Health and Family Welfare Medical to promote Wellness Tourism a nd (iv) the Ministry of 
Information & Broadcasting for Film Tourism.

and marketing of various Spiritual Tourism destinations to attract both domestic and 
international visitors.   The Ministry is also promoting various tourism destinations through its 3 
Schemes, namely, Swadesh Darshan Scheme (SDS), PRASHAD, and Central Financial 
Assistance for Central Agencies.   Under the SDS, 15 thematic circuits have been identified an d 
76 projects have been  sanctioned to date. Out of this 23 sanctioned projects worth Rs. 1365.01 
Crore belong to Spiritual Circuit, including Krishna Circuit, Buddhist Circuit, Spiritual Circuit, 
Ramayana Circuit, and Tirthankara Circuit. The revamped SDS 2.0 has 55 destinations identified 
across 32 States/UTs for development. The Committee was also informed of various successful 
projects of the Ministry under the SDS 1.0 in the States of Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Puducherry, 
Tripura, Uttarakhand, and Vadnagar (Gujarat).

infrastructure for pilgrimage/spiritual tourism, has been allocated Rs. 1630.05 Crores for 46

digital initiatives for tourism promotion, the Ministry has also set up the ‘Utsav Portal’ to 
provide live streaming of various destinations and their festivals. The Committee was further 
informed that the Ministry is promoting pote ntial tourist spots through its website as well as 
organizing tourism -related National Festivals such as ‘Bharat Parv,’ and ‘Paryatan Parv,’ 
conducting online and social media campaigns.  
16. The Ministry further informed that it is working on identifying 10 to 12 tourist 
destinations for which it has created a value chain focusing on tourism mapping. It is also 
looking into incentivizing ‘Green tourism’, which has been one of the major points of discussion 

154 
 
in G-20 meetings. In the G-20 Tourism Working Group, the Ministry created the Goa Road Map 
giving recommendations for Sustainable and Responsible Tourism, best digitization practices of 
various countries, skill development, and tourism Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises

 Developing a very strong Tourism Rating System in India to curb manipulation.

Details of Information given to the Committee by the representatives of DFCCIL through

1.  DFCCIL is a  PSU of the Ministry of Railways  and is responsible for funding, constructing 
and commissioning of DFCs, their Operation and Maintenance, business development for higher 
rail, modal share, reduction in logistics costs and development of New DFCs. 
2. Indian Railways’ network of Golden Quadrilateral (Delhi – Chennai – Mumbai – Howrah) 
along the diagonal rail routes accounts for just 16% of the railway route, but carries 52% of the 
railway’s passenger traffic and earns 58% of revenue of freight traffic.   Railway Modal Share in 
the developed countries is more than 45% whereas in India, it is about 26%.    . 
3.    The total stretch of the WDFC and EDFC is 3,300 km which passes through 9 States and 72 
Districts. 11,000 hectares of land has been acquired by DFCCIL throughout the entire stretch of 
India and more than 250 million cubic metre of earthwork has to be done for the construction of 
this project. DFCCIL has currently been provided with an allocation of Rs. 1,24,000 Crore out of 
which Rs. 51,200 Cr. is jointly funded by World Bank and Indian Railways for the E astern DFC 
of length 1,337 kms (Ludhiana via Dadri to Sonnagar) and Rs. 72,800 Cr. is jointly funded by 
Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and Indian Railways for the Western DFC of 
length 1,506 kms (Mumbai to Dadri). The remaining 538 km in EDFC is yet to be sanctioned.  
4. 30% land out of the total 70% acquired, is Greenfield.   4.265m container height in WDFC has 
been provided to give wider and bigger stock in the same capacity, whereas, in EDFC, it has 
been envisaged that it would be better to  have a wagon height of 1.5m. The current Axle load is 
proposed to be increased to 32.5 tonnes from the present 25 tonnes. The Signaling system is 
provided at every two kilometres while the ‘Kavach’ System is yet to be installed.  
5.        DFCCIL has constructed 543 major bridges,  4,643 minor bridges and 53 Rail flyovers. It 
has also constructed 304 Road Over Bridges (ROBs), and 557 Rail Over Bridges (RUBs), due to 
which 861 level crossings have been eliminated to enable seamless transportation. DFCCIL has  
built 114 Greenfield Stations, and the state -of-the-art Western and Eastern Operation Control 
Centres at Ahmedabad and Prayagraj respectively. Indian Railways is also upgrading its own 
feeder routes connecting to the DFCs to ensure that the traffic origin ating from non-DFC routes, 
but passing through it is routed through DFCs. Existing freight trains can also move on the DFC 
tracks.  DFCCIL has also proposed to develop New DFCs of about 4,315 km in length.  
6.        The DFCs would be able to carry faster,  heavier, longer hauls. DFCs have achieved more 
than 60 kmph average speed as compared to goods trains average speed of 25 kmph. In the 
Indian railway network, freight operations are marred by the preferences given to the passenger 
trains due to traffic congestion.  In the DFC train operations will become smooth and a scheduled 
time table would be possible. When the entire DFC network becomes operational, it will save 
457 million -ton CO2 over a 30 -year period and it would also lead to quantum jump in 

158 
 
transportation capacity i.e. 120 trains each way, reduction in logistics costs, connectivity to 
private sidings and freight terminals as well as major and minor ports.   
7.        The DFCCIL will construct 6 private freight terminals on PPP basis which will beco me 
loading points for line capacity augmentation. 
8.      The DFCCIL is working on two MMLPs at Dadri and Rewari in coordination with the 
National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC) and MMLPs are being 
developed with the coordination of various Ministries/Departments.  
9. The sanctioned strength of DFCCIL is 5,998 but DFCCIL is operating with approximately 
3,000 personnel only.

1 
 
 
REPORT 
 
Introduction 
 
The Indian Civil Aviation sector has witnessed an e xponential growth in passenger traffic over 
the past few years and a corresponding increase in the numbers of Airports, Aircrafts and flight 
routes. The Civil Aviation sector is set to grow at  a fast pace in the next few years, since it is an 
area of focus for the Government. New domestic airp orts have been operationalised and air 
travel routes have also been initiated, with the la unch of Regional Connectivity Scheme-‘Ude 
Desh ka Aam Nagrik’ (RCS-UDAN), which envisages to make air travel affordable for the 
common man. The growth in the Civil Aviation sector  is contingent on the affordability of 
airfares, besides other factors. The fixing of airf ares is an issue of cardinal importance for all 
major stakeholders - the Government, the airline industry as well as the common man.  
 
2. In view of the significance of the subject, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture decided  to take up the subject ‘Issue of Fixing of 
Airfares’ for examination and Report. To deliberate  upon the various issues related to 
rationalisation of airfares, it was imperative to t ake into consideration the views of the various 
stakeholders viz., Ministry of Civil Aviation, vari ous private airlines and Association of Private 
Airport Operators (APAO). The Committee, therefore,  heard the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 
8
th  May, 2023. The Committee also held discussions wit h various private airlines viz., Air Asia, 
Air India, GoFirst, Indigo, SpiceJet & Vistara and APAO, in its meeting held on 5 th  April, 2023. 
The Committee once again heard the views of various  private airlines viz., Air Asia, Air India, 
Indigo, SpiceJet & Vistara and APAO, to seek clarifications on certain issues, in its meeting held 
on 29 th  May, 2023. During its Study Visit to Mumbai and Go a during 5 th  to 8 th  July, 2023, the 
Committee also discussed the issue of surge in airfares with the representatives of the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation in Goa on 8 th  July, 2023.     
 

2 
 
I 
REGULATORY PROVISIONS  
 
Airfare Regulations in the Past 
3. The Ministry in its background note, informed th e Committee of the following 
regulations on Airfares, that existed in the past:- 
 
• The Air Corporations Act, 1953 contained the provis ion that the Corporations, with the 
previous approval of the Central Government, will d etermine and levy fares and freight 
rates and other charges for or in respect of the ca rriage of passengers and goods on air 
transport services operated by it.  
 
• In August, 1975, Rule 135B of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 on changes in tariff of fares, rates 
and charges and production of records was introduce d vide  GSR 2386. It contained the 
provisions that no change shall be made in fares, r ates and charges or in classifications, 
rules, regulations, practices or services affecting  such fares, rates and charges or value of 
the services including any change in the terms or conditions of the commission payable to 
the passenger or cargo sales agents except after pr evious approval by the Director 
General. The application for such changes was requi red to be made to the Director 
General at least thirty days in advance for approval.  
 
• On 24 
th  March, 1994, with the repeal of Air Corporations A ct, 1953, the above provision 
was dispensed with by the Government. The Indian do mestic aviation was totally 
deregulated. Airlines were allowed to freely induct  capacity with any aircraft type, select 
whatever markets and network they wish to service a nd operate and also fix any fares. 
However, Indian Airlines continued to approach the Government and obtain prior 
permission from the Ministry of Civil Aviation befo re affecting any fare increase in 
accordance with the Ministry’s directive dated 31 st  August, 1998. Indian Airlines and 
Alliance Air were not required to comply with this requirement by the Ministry on 3 rd  
May, 2001 and permitted to decide the fares based o n dynamic and market-oriented 
pricing policy. 
 
• In September, 2004, Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules,  1937 was amended vide  GSR 636 
(E) and the above provision contained in Rule 135B was omitted. The provisions of the 
Rule 135 were then limited to having determination of fares for international air 
transportation having regard to all relevant factor s, including the cost of operation, 
reasonable profit and the general prevailing tariff and upkeep of tariff records. 
 
4. The Committee notes the Airfare regulations that  existed in the past and observes 
that the Air Corporations Act, 1953 required the va rious airline corporations to seek 
approval of Central Government for fixing airfares.  Thereafter, on 21 
st  March, 1994, the 

3 
 
said Act was repealed and the Indian Domestic Aviation Sector was totally deregulated and 
the airlines had the freedom to fix airfares.  
 
5. The Committee notes that as per the airfare regu lations existing earlier, the airfares 
were fully regulated by the Government which had pu t in place a mechanism to keep 
airfares under check. Thereafter, deregulation of a irfares effectively came into effect from 
21 
st  March, 1994 with the repeal of the Air Corporation  Act, 1953 and the various airlines 
were free to fix airfares.  
  
Existing Legal Provisions  
6. On 16 
th  April, 2009, vide  GSR 254(E), Rule 135 was again amended to cover as pects for 
domestic air transport also and display of fare com ponents. The Ministry also informed that at 
present, airfares are not controlled by the Governm ent. Airlines offer fares at various levels 
which are demand driven based on market dynamics an d as the demand goes up the seats on 
lower fare levels get filled. This is a global prac tice in the civil aviation sector and dynamic 
pricing defines the strategic framework. Day-to-day  tactical changes in pricing are made to 
respond to demand/supply and market dynamics throug h the Inventory Management process of 
various airlines. 
 
Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937  
7. The aforesaid Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 19 37, as amended on 16 
th  April, 2009, as 
regards fixing of air tariff is as follows:- 
 
135. Tariff – (1) Every air transport undertaking o perating in accordance with sub-rule (1) 
and (2) of rule 134, shall establish tariff having regard to all relevant factors, including the 
cost of operation, characteristics of service, reas onable profit and the generally prevailing 
tariff.  
 
(2) Every air transport undertaking shall cause to be published the tariff established by him 
under sub-rule (1) in his website or two daily news papers, and shall display such tariff in a 
conspicuous part of his office and in the office of his agent, if any.  
 
(2A) The tariff to be published under sub-rule (2) or advertised in any other way shall 
show the following particulars, namely:–  
 
(a) the total amount payable by a passenger; and  
(b) a complete break-up of the total amount, indica ting the fare, tax, fees or any other 
charge, if any, separately.  
 
 Explanation. – For the purposes of this sub-rule, –  
 
(a) tax means the amount payable to the Government; and  

4 
 
(b) fees means the amount payable to the service pr oviders for provision of any 
service or facility to the passengers.  
(2B) The particulars mentioned in sub-rule (2A) sha ll also be mentioned in the passenger 
ticket.  
 
(3) Every air transport undertaking shall maintain all records relating to tariff established 
by him under sub-rule (1) in such manner and in suc h form as may be specified by the 
Director General, and on demand by the Director Gen eral shall produce such records 
before the Director-General for inspection.  
(4) Where the Director-General is satisfied that an y air transport undertaking has 
established excessive or predatory tariff under sub -rule (1) or has indulged in oligopolistic 
practice, he may, by order, issue directions to such air transport undertaking.  
(5) Every direction issued under sub-rule (4) shall  be complied with by such air transport 
undertaking. 
 
8. The Committee notes the amendment in Rule 135 of  the Aircraft Rules, 1937 on 16 
th  
April, 2009, which presently forms the basis of the legislation for airfare regulations. It also 
notes that as per the Rule 135(1), the airlines sha ll establish tariff, keeping in mind factors 
such as reasonable profit besides cost of operation , characteristics of service and generally 
prevailing tariff, to rationalise airfares despite its deregulation, consequent upon repeal of 
Air Corporations Act, 1953. 
 
9. The Committee also observes that Rule 135(2) req uires the publication of the tariff 
by the airlines on its website/ daily newspapers or  displaying it conspicuously in their 
office/ or the agent’s office. Further, Section 135 (2A) requires the airlines to show the total 
amount payable by the passenger including the break up such as taxes, fees for services/ 
facilities or other charges, which should be mentio ned in the passenger ticket vide Rule 135 
(2B).  
 
10. The Committee notes another significant require ment in Rule 135(3), wherein every 
airline is required to maintain all records relatin g to tariff and the requirement to produce 
such records to Directorate General of Civil Aviati on (DGCA) for inspection. The 
Committee observes that the aforesaid Rule provides  for supervision and inspection of 
DGCA (Ministry of Civil Aviation) on air tariffs being fixed by the airlines. 
 
11. Rule 135 (4) also empowers the DGCA to issue di rections to airlines, if it is satisfied 
that the airlines have charged excessive/ predatory  airfares or indulged in oligopolistic 
practice. Further, as per Rule 135 (5), the aforesa id directions of DGCA have to be 
compiled with by the airline concerned. 
 
12. The Committee, therefore, observes that ever si nce the amendment made in Rule 
135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 in April, 2009, suf ficient legislative safeguards have been 

5 
 
made in the Aircraft Rules, 1937, to ensure that ai rfares are affordable and in case of any 
violation by the airlines, the Government can take action against the said airline regardless 
of the deregulation of the airfares, due to repeal of Air Corporation Act, 1953. The 
Committee calls upon the DGCA, Ministry of Civil Av iation to safeguard the interests of 
the air commuters by invoking the overriding powers vested on it in the Rules. 
 
Power of DGCA to Regulate Tariffs 
13. During its deliberations, the Committee enquire d into the mechanism adopted by the 
Ministry to regulate tariffs, based on the Rule 135  of Aircraft Rules, 1937. The Ministry replied 
that Tariff Monitoring Unit (TMU), as set up by DGC A, monitors airfares on selected 50 routes 
on a random basis by using airlines websites on mon thly basis to ensure that the airlines do not 
charge airfares outside the range declared by them.  During unforeseen circumstances like floods, 
natural calamities, civil unrest, etc., the fares o n the affected sectors are monitored to ensure 
compliance of prevailing regulations on airfare. Th e monitoring of airfares has revealed that all 
scheduled domestic airlines are displaying route-wise and category-wise fares on their respective 
websites in compliance to the applicable regulation . Airfares are monitored using airlines 
websites. The analysis has shown that the airfares remained well within the fare bucket uploaded 
by the airlines on their respective websites.  
 
14. The Ministry further informed that an analysis of the monitoring of airfares showed that 
the percentage of tickets sold in the highest fare bucket on majority sectors is minuscule, barring 
a very few sectors which may be on account of seasonality and capacity constraints, etc. 
 
15. The Ministry also apprised that while the Gover nment no longer regulates the fares that 
are charged, it is ensured that considerable inform ation is provided to the public in a transparent 
manner with respect to airline fares and DGCA Air T ransport Circulars have been issued from 
time to time in this regard. Air Transport Circular s 05 of 2009; 02 of 2010; and 03 of 2013 are 
placed at Annexure-I.   
 
16. During its deliberations, the Committee also en quired the reasons for not empowering 
DGCA to regulate tariffs based on the data generate d by the Tariff Monitoring Unit and whether 
the Ministry proposes to empower DGCA to take neces sary action (including regulating tariffs) 
in response to the data generated by it. The Minist ry explained that as per Section 4 A of the 
Aircraft Act 1934, DGCA is primarily responsible fo r carrying out the safety oversight and 
regulatory functions in respect of matters specifie d in this Act or in the rules made thereunder. 
Further, with the repeal of Air Corporation Act, 19 53 in March 1994, the process of airfare 
approval by Government has been dispensed with. As per the prevailing regulations, airfares are 
not regulated by the Government. Under the provisio n of Sub Rule (1) of Rule 135 of the 
Aircraft Rules, 1937, every air transport undertaki ng engaged in scheduled air services requires 
to establish tariff having regard to all relevant f actors, including cost of operation, characteristic  
of services, reasonable profit and the generally prevailing tariff.  
 

6 
 
17. The Committee observes that DGCA has a Tariff M onitoring Unit that monitors 
airfares on certain routes at regular intervals to ensure that the airlines do not charge 
airfares outside a range declared by them. However, the DGCA does not have any power to 
regulate tariffs based on the data generated by the  Tariff Monitoring Unit as the process of 
airfare regulation has been dispensed with, consequ ent upon the repeal of the Air 
Corporation Act, 1953.  
 
18. The Committee notes that Section 135(3) of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 empowers the 
DGCA to inspect the records of tariff as produced b y the airline operators and also 
empowers it to issue directions in case it has esta blished excessive tariff [Section 135(4)]. 
The Committee observes that though Tariff Monitorin g Unit of DGCA has been setup to 
maintain oversight, yet the airlines are charging e xcessively, leading to surge in airfares. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should e volve a mechanism to reconcile 
between ‘tariff monitoring’ by DGCA and ‘deregulati on of airfare’ to tilt the balance in 
favour of empowering the DGCA to regulate air tariff as per Rule 135(3) and expanding its 
responsibility beyond monitoring tariff only. The C ommittee desires to know whether a 
Unit or Agency like Tariff Monitoring Unit (TMU) ex ists in other countries as well and 
mechanism adopted by them to regulate fares. 
 
19. The Committee is also aware that the Securities  and Exchange Board of India 
(SEBI), an autonomous body, has been setup for regu lating the securities market and to 
protect the interest of investors. The Committee op ines that on similar lines, the feasibility 
of setting up of a monitoring and controlling body under the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
may be examined, to monitor and keep a check on the  surge in airfares to protect the 
interests of the commuting public. The Committee, t herefore, recommends the Ministry to 
constitute a separate monitoring body like the SEBI , with quasi-judicial powers to enforce 
the collection of reasonable airfares from the passengers. 
 
20. The Ministry also informed the Committee that t he aviation sector is a capital intensive 
business and the airlines operate in an extremely c ompetitive environment. The airline industry 
has to face unforeseen challenges to remain in busi ness and it has been observed that many

Reasonable Profit, Generally Prevailing Tariff and Mechanism followed for Fixing 
Airfares 
29. The Committee enquired whether the Ministry of Civil Aviation has laid down any rules 
to ensure that airlines calculate ‘reasonable profi t’ and ‘generally prevailing tariff’ in a fair and 
transparent manner. The Ministry clarified that wit h the repeal of Air Corporation Act in March 
1994, the process of airfare approval by Government  has been dispensed with. As per prevailing 
regulation, airfares are not regulated by the Gover nment. Under the provision of Sub Rule (1) of 
Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, every air tra nsport undertaking engaged in scheduled air 
services require to establish tariff having regard to all relevant factors, including cost of 
operation, characteristic of services, reasonable profit and the generally prevailing tariff. Airlines 
are free to charge airfares as per their operationa l viability. Government does not interfere either 
in commercial aspects of airline or fixing of airfa re by them. Airlines remain compliant to the 
regulatory provisions of Sub-Rule 2 of Rule 135 as long as the fare charged by them does not 
exceed the fare bucket established and displayed on their website.  
 
30. The Ministry explained that the term ‘reasonabl e profit’ is embedded under the provision 
of Sub-Rule (1) of Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, under the “Tariff”. There is no separate 
rule or any other guideline defining ‘reasonable pr ofit’ and ‘generally prevailing tariff’. These 
words are understood as per the common understanding. 
 

9 
 
31. The Committee also enquired from the Ministry w hether there is any mechanism to 
impose penalties on airlines in cases of overchargi ng. The Ministry explained that airfares are 
not regulated by the Government. The airfares are c ompetitive in nature and are subjected to 
rules framed under the Competition Act, 2002 under the purview of the Competition 
Commission of India (CCI). 
 
32. The Committee notes that though the term ‘reaso nable profit’ is given under Rule 
135(1) of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, yet there is no  specific definition or Rule or any other 
guidelines to define it and these expressions are l iable to be misunderstood, besides 
encouraging arbitrary actions. The Committee is of the opinion that the term ‘reasonable 
profit’ should be clearly defined in the Rules, tak ing into account various financial and 
operational factors, as it is the most significant aspect for controlling surge in airfares, 
which affects the common man.  
 
33. The Committee also enquired from the various ai rlines during its meetings held on 5 th  
April and 29 th  May, 2023 as to the methodology used by airlines t o calculate the quantum of 
‘reasonable profit’ and ‘generally prevailing tarif f, the minimum number of tickets needed to be 
sold on a particular route for airlines to break-ev en and beyond this break-even point, the 
mechanism for pricing tickets to maintain ‘reasonab le profit’. The Committee also sought 
information on the Capital Investment; Working Capi tal; Revenue Expenditure; Fixed Cost; 
Operating Expenditure; Net Income; and Profit/Loss,  in respect of the airlines. The replies of the 
individual airlines are at Annexure-II . 
 
34. The representative of Air Asia stated that prof itability of any route is moderated by the 
natural demand – supply dynamics of that route. Mos t airlines in India have struggled to make 
any profits as a result of high competition between  airlines resulting in low fares in the Indian 
market. Generally prevailing airfare tariff on a pa rticular route is a result of the demand-supply 
balance. As regards, the minimum number of tickets needed to be sold on a particular route for 
airlines to break-even, the representative stated that the number of tickets to be sold on any route 
to achieve break-even (“Break-even Seat Factor”) de pends on the fares being charged and the 
cost of operations on that route. Therefore Break-e ven Seat Factor varies by route, seasonality 
and total demand-supply in the market and hence is difficult to ascertain a fixed number of seats 
for the break-even. Since most airlines in India ha ve been unprofitable for most parts of their 
existence, the airlines are clearly not even able t o achieve the break-even point. If one looks at 
the average fares realised in the market and compar e them with the cost of the operations, the 
‘break-even seat factor’ comes out to be an infeasible figure of greater than100%.  
 
35. The representative of Air India informed the Co mmittee that airlines globally work on a 
Cost Recovery Model rather than on a set target to achieve reasonable profit. The airline pricing 
is highly elastic. Pricing of air tickets by Air In dia is pegged against key competitors on the 
given route, keeping in view relative product stren gths. Reasonable market fares have been 
formulated by Air India taking into consideration the underlying factors:   

10 
 
• Fares offered by competitors in a highly dynamic market. 
• Product offerings, 
• Seasonality (as per practice adopted by all airlines worldwide),  
• Flight frequency, timings, direct / indirect operat ions, Product, Competitors’ activities, 
Traffic Flows.  
• Market demand 
 
36. Further, the minimum number of tickets to be so ld depends on cost of operation based on 
type of equipment and also price of ticket. The num ber of tickets required to be sold can, 
therefore, vary by market demand, seasonality, prev alent fares and product offerings. Air India 
operates many routes which are for building future demand and in this case, they generally incur 
losses irrespective of number of tickets sold. Hence, currently no such system exists in Air India.  
 
37. The representative of GoFirst stated that ‘reas onable profit’, is to recover all cost related 
to running the flight operations both variable and fixed nature. “Generally prevailing tariff /uni201F are 
the fares at market driven demand at which the tick ets are sold in advance through the 365 days 
window. They added that each different route has di fferent break-even, however, to break-even 
at contribution level average required tickets to b e sold at more than 85%. Therefore, beyond 
break-even point, fares for balance seats are priced to recover all cost. 
 
38. The representative of Indigo informed the Commi ttee that they do not set a target 
“reasonable profit”. Demand for air travel is highl y price sensitive and varies due to multiple 
factors, including the price of the air ticket. The y endeavour to set prices in line with estimation 
of demand and calibrate the same on basis of off-ta ke of seats, changes in cost, estimated cost 
recovery, need to stimulate demand, network feeds /  flows, etc. They also stated that Indigo, like 
most airlines across the world, follows the practic e of ‘revenue management’ which involves 
varying prices according to changes in demand and a vailable capacity. They also informed that 
other industries such as hotels, both in India and abroad, also practice revenue management 
techniques. Further, revenue management takes into account demand & supply and also 
variations in demand. An airline seat is perishable  inventory, which means that once a flight has 
departed, the unsold seat inventory has no value.  
 
39. The representative of SpiceJet stated that pric ing aspects are dependent on the market 
situation and the prevailing conditions. These amou nts cannot be quantified into a specific 
figure/ range as the same varies basis type of airc raft, market situation, the number of seats sold 
on different fare bucket basis market dynamics and offers etc. 
 
40. The representative of Vistara informed the Comm ittee that reasonable profit and 
generally prevailing tariff is based on the operati onal costs as well as the ongoing fares in the 
Indian and foreign aviation environment. They added that number of tickets needed to be sold on 
a particular route for them to break-even, depends on the market demand and the available 

11 
 
supply based on which Revenue Management System (RM S) system allocates the inventory on 
every price points. In many routes, airlines may no t break even due to low demand and over 
capacity. The pricing of tickets are based on inven tory allocation. RMS does the allocation of

41. The Committee notes the replies of the represen tatives of various airlines as regards 
its query on the mechanism adopted by them to calcu late the quantum of ‘reasonable 
profit’. The airlines had commented that the prevai ling air tariff on a particular route is a 
result of demand-supply balance. Besides, airlines work on a ‘Cost Recovery Model’, so as 
to recover all costs related to flight operations, rather than on a set target to achieve 
‘reasonable profit’. One of the airlines had also s tated that they do not set a target 
‘reasonable profit’ and the practice of ‘Revenue Ma nagement’ is followed which takes into

42. As regards, the Committee’s query regarding the  minimum number of tickets 
needed to be sold on a particular route for airline s to break-even, the airlines were of the 
opinion that since most of the airlines have been u nprofitable for most parts of their 
existence, the airlines were not able to achieve br eak-even point. Hence, currently, no such 
system exists in India. Airline representatives opi ned that the number of tickets sold for 
break-even depends on demand-supply dynamics based on which Revenue Management 
System does the pricing.  
 
43. The Committee observes that though the concept of establishing tariffs on basis of 
‘reasonable profit’ is ingrained in the Rule 135(1)  of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, yet none of 
the airlines has adopted a mechanism to calculate t he quantum of ‘reasonable profit’. All 
the airlines are instead following the demand-suppl y dynamics through the ‘Revenue 
Management System’ and hence, airfares are fixed accordingly.  
 
44. The Committee understands that the fixing of ai rfares depends on various 
conditions which are subject to variation of the de mand-supply dynamics of the market 
and the airlines have to account for these factors for maintaining economy of operations. 
The Committee is, however, of the opinion that a ba lance has to be maintained between the 
commercial interests of the airlines as well as the  interests of the passengers. It is of the 
opinion that to fix airfares at reasonable and affordable rates, the airlines need to adopt the 
concept of ‘reasonable profit’ drawing from the bes t international practices. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry in consultation with the airlines 
should devise a mechanism or a formula, so that the  concept of ‘reasonable profit’ as 
provided explicitly in Rule 135(1) of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 is adhered to.

52. The Committee noted that incorrect information is often published by the airlines on their

misleading the public with incorrect information by  tricking them into paying more under the 
guise of selling “last seats”. It enquired from the  various airlines the reasons for publishing

publication of information regarding fares/seats; a nd other safeguards taken to ensure that such

57. In reply, the Ministry apprised that the guidel ines for recognition/ renewal or extension as 
an approved travel agent/ agency are issued by the Ministry of Tourism, which has laid down the 
conditions and procedures to be followed between a travel agent and an airline. The Directorate 
General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is not empowered t o approve or disapprove the tariff charged 
by booking portals, as the tariff established by ai rlines is not required to be submitted to DGCA 
for approval, as Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 is related to airfare only. 
 
58. As per clarification of the Ministry of Civil A viation, the term “Commission”, 
“Transaction Fees”, “Convenience Fees” or any other terms used for the purpose means the same 
i.e. payment of remuneration to the intermediaries for the services rendered by them. Therefore, 
all these terms are treated as “Commission”, mentioned in the existing rule 135 of Aircraft Rules, 
1937 as a part of tariff and are to be determined b y the airlines. The aforesaid order further states 
that DGCA cannot lay down quantum of commission pay able by airlines to agents. It is upto the 
airlines to take a decision in this regard in consu ltation with intermediaries taking into account 
various commercial factors such as the market condi tions, the cost of the intermediary’s 
establishments, etc. and statutory definition of tariff.

multiple fare levels as indicated below, for a single flight which is the practice followed globally. 
(i) Each RBD (fare level) is assigned a specific nu mber of seats (inventory).  
(ii) At any point of time, one RBD is open for sale  based on the number of seats still 
 left in that RBD.  
(iii) As seats assigned to an RBD is exhausted, tha t fare level is closed and the higher 
 RBD is opened.  
(iv) Thus, the current selling price of tickets mov es to the next RBD level. RBDs are 
 based on the internal practices of each airline, w hich are always aligned to the 
 market structure and its dynamics. 
 
64. Airlines use RBDs to manage the demand 
vis-à-vis  the limited supply of seats to create 
value for the passengers. As the service and capaci ty offerings in the different classes differ, the 
pricing is done accordingly. Airlines offer differe ntial fares under different brands by taking into 
consideration the service attributes attached to th e brands to offer more choice and freedom to 
the passengers to choose and decide which product to consume. 
 
65. As demand for air travel is highly price sensit ive and varies due to multiple factors, 
including the price of the air ticket, airlines end eavour to set prices in line with an estimation of 
demand and calibrate the same on the basis of off-t ake of seats, changes in cost (including fuel), 
estimated cost recovery, need to stimulate demand a nd network feeds/flows. These prices are 
stated in “fare levels / buckets” with number of se ats being varied in each bucket in line with 
revenue management practices. 
 
66. The primary factors based on which specific buc kets or price points are open for sale are 
market conditions - reference to competition landsc ape, frequency, time of the flights, 
seasonality, etc. Seat allocation per pricing point is dynamic in nature and there are countless sell 
and cancel transactions taking place every second f rom multiple sources over the entire network. 
Most of the airlines being commercial organisations, the inventory team endeavours to maximise 
the revenue by judiciously monitoring demand and supply.

67. The Committee, after analysis of International Journals on the subject, found that 
International Air Transportation Association (IATA) ’s Recommended Practices (RPs) are only a 
suggested framework to harmonize industry practices  in the air-transport sector. While IATA is 
not a governmental organization and has, therefore,  no competence for legislation, their 
Recommended Practices are internationally recognize d references and generally have a non-
binding character.  
 
68. Some airlines have adopted these RPs or general  conditions as minimum requirements in 
their Conditions of Carriage or have modified them to suit their own commercial practices. 
Hence, different terms and conditions exist in the aviation sector for various airlines. However, 
the non-binding IATA rules or RPs as international standards are not prioritized in favour of 
national law, but, on the contrary, have to comply with the national law.

Effect of Seasonality/Holidays on Airfares  
78. The Ministry highlighted that India has a highl y seasonal market. Traffic is usually high 
in the months of May and June. Through mid-July the  international traffic flows are high, thus 
contributing to the domestic feed as well. From Jul y to September is traditionally leaner period 
as travel is restricted due to monsoon and other re ligious reasons. In October, with the festive 
season starting from Dussera, traffic picks up agai n and by the middle of January the demand 
diminishes. Till about the last week of April, this  trend of softening of demand continues and 
again, due to summer holidays, the demand increases.  
 
79. The Committee was further informed that Air tra vellers are extremely price-sensitive. 
Price is the primary driver to pick an airline espe cially for leisure travellers. All airlines compete  
on price with other carriers in the respective mark ets. Airlines adopt dynamic pricing by 
changing prices often depending on the day of the w eek, time of day, and number of days before 
the flight factoring in different components such a s, how many seats a flight has, departure time, 
and average cancellations on similar flights. Dynam ic pricing is crucial in determining how 
airlines improve their revenue per flight. 
 
80. The Committee, during its deliberations, highli ghted the concerns expressed by 
passengers at the surge of airfares during festive seasons, summer vacations, when a large 
number of people travel across the Country for reli gious/ leisure purposes or other reasons 
and thus promoting domestic tourism and boosting the economy. The Committee notes that 
affordable air transport is a must for the growth o f tourism in India, which is presently 
reviving after facing a steep decline due to Covid pandemic. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry may devise suitable monitoring mechanism to keep a check on the sudden 
surge in prices during the festive season or holida ys or natural calamities, as it has a 
negative impact on tourism.

1. Schedule advantage / disadvantage – Flights with  better timings see higher customer

2. Available Seats – In case a few seats are available on a flight, the fares may be higher.

92. The representative also contended that there ar e two main propositions on which budget 
or Low-Cost-Carrier (LCC), differ from the Full Service Carrier (FSC):  
• In LCC, there is only economy class in the cabin. N ot having a business class helps LCC 
with more seats per flight thereby reducing the cos t per seat and hence offering lower 
fares; and  
• LCCs offer unbundled product, i.e., meals and any o ther auxiliary services like lounge 
facility, which are not offered as part of the fare  but can be bought separately. This again 
helps offer lower fares and only the customers who value auxiliary services like meals 
have to pay for such services.
