that the distinction made by the Ministry regarding  the monuments lost to 
urbanisation/reservoirs and 24 monuments which are untraceable is an academic distinction 
since monuments lost to urbanisation/reservoirs are  as irrecoverable as the ones which are 
presently untraceable with scant hope of being foun d in future.  Moreover, the fact that the 
ASI had been unable to prevent the loss of the 14 m onuments to urbanisation and 12 to 
reservoirs/dams and only located them after the stu dy by CAG suggests that the ASI had no 
cognisance of these monuments prior to the study. The number of monuments lost from public 
viewing must therefore be held to be 50 taking into  account those lost to urbanisation or 
reservoirs.  The ASI has assured that the remaining  42 of the 92 monuments exist physically 
but the Committee would like to know whether these monuments exist in their entirety and 
undamaged or whether the ASI has only managed to lo cate some remains and ruins of such 
monuments.   
(Para 11)  
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 To ascertain the conservation status of these m onuments, they shall be again inspected 
through the field offices of ASI. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Ministry has stated that there is no term ca lled “Missing Monuments” in the 
AMASR Act and the term only came into existence as it was used by the Audit team on their 
Report. The Committee opines that the AMASR Act pro vides for the preservation and 
protection of ancient historical monuments and it would have been inconsistent to include the 
concept of “Missing Monuments” in the Act.  That th e situation warrants the use of such 
phrases only serves to underline the apathy of the Ministry and ASI regarding the 
preservation of our historical monuments.  The Mini stry has also stated that the exercise of 
removing the untraceable monuments under Section 35  of the AMASR Act has not been 
initiated by the ASI as there are chances that some  of these monuments shall be traced out in 
near future. The Committee observes that Section 35  of the AMASR Act, 1958 has the 
provision to issue notification only for such CPMs which have as per the opinion of the 
Central Government have ceased to be of national im portance. The monuments which have 
become “untraceable” have become so due to official  apathy and may not have ceased to be 

7 
 
of national importance had they been existing.  The  situation of a “Missing Monument” 
cannot be automatically equated with loss of its hi storical importance.  The Committee 
recommends that the Untraceable Monuments may not b e removed from the list of Centrally 
Protected Monuments by taking recourse to Section 3 5 as that Section provides the exclusion 
only of such monuments which have in the opinion of the Central Government ceased to be of 
national importance.  In fact, there is the danger that in case of such removal, there would be 
no imperative to find the untraceable monument and it would be well and truly lost to 
posterity. Since untraceable monuments also cannot continue to be on the Protected list, the 
Committee recommends that the list of Untraceable M onuments may be maintained as such 
and if necessary, the AMASR Act may be amended to include this terminology.   
(Para 12)  
Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 The observation shall be taken into considerati on while amending the AMASR Act. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee feels that a thorough review of th e AMASR Act in consultation with all 
stakeholders and State Governments is the need of t he hour. The Committee, therefore, 
appreciates the process initiated by the Ministry o f Culture to amend the AMASR Act. The 
Committee agrees with the view that having the same  limits for all monuments for prohibited 
area and regulated area for restricting/regulating construction-related activities near the 
monument, is not a practical approach as the requir ement for such limitations could vary a 
lot depending on various factors specific to each m onument. The Committee, therefore, feels 
that the upcoming amendment which provides for such  monument-specific prohibited and 
regulated areas is much needed and hopes that once the amendment is passed, all necessary 
steps are taken to ensure that the monument-specifi c limits are decided upon for each 
Centrally Protected Monument at the earliest. The C ommittee notes that the ASI would be 
surveying all 3693 monuments while delineating monu ment specific protected and regulated 
limits and desires that a Report of the survey may be submitted to the Committee. However, 
the provisions of the Act may be strictly adhered t o in terms of the prohibited areas around 
the monument and even Government officials violating the provisions should be prosecuted.  
(Para 17)  
Reply of the Ministry  
3.1 For dealing with the NOCs cases in the circles and RD offices, the google and Bhuvan 
maps, wherever possible to delineate, were created for  showing protected, prohibited and 
regulated limit of the monuments. Since ASI is work ing on the amendment of the AMASR

Recommendation/Observation

Report on ‘Creation of Regulatory Framework for pro tection of Historical Sites and 
Monuments’:  
The Committee fails to see why a person living in t he Regulated Area of a CPM 
should be required to seek permission from the Comp etent Authority under the 
AMASR Rules for carrying out innocuous maintenance activities such as filling of 
cracks, whitewashing, replacement of windows etc. T he Committee feels that such 
uncalled-for interference makes lives harder for pe ople living nearby the monuments 
and could slowly cause feelings of anguish towards the monument itself. Given the 
large number of monuments across the country and th e limited budgetary resources 
available with the Government, it is pertinent that  people residing near the

placing such unnecessary curbs and implementing the m is a wastage of limited

(Para 18)

security guards to protect our rich cultural herita ge. It is the bounden duty of the 
Government of the day to protect our cultural herit age sites. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that budget may be provided by the Gover nment to appoint 7000 personnel for 
protection of the Monuments which may be later alte red as per the study conducted by IIT, 
Delhi. In view of this worrying state of affairs, t he Committee is of the strong view that the 
budgetary allocation available with the Ministry/AS I for safeguarding our Centrally 
Protected Monuments needs a serious relook. The Com mittee recommends that the 
Ministry/ASI may conduct an urgent thorough assessm ent of the security requirements and 
budgetary allocation required for the same and a st rong case may be made to the Ministry of 
Finance requesting allocation of additional funds f or this purpose so as to ensure a basic 
state of protection for all Centrally Protected Mon uments across the country to preserve 
them for generations to come.  
(Para 43.14.3)

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF

Quality of Roads  
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should t ake necessary steps for the 
deployment of MQCVs in the remaining States for bet ter inspection and quality

The Committee also feels that the Ministry needs to  come up with a better policy for

(Para 4.6)

(Para 4.8)

The Committee notes that the prices of items at res taurants, food courts, dhabas are

proper implementation. Further, the Ministries must  work in spreading awareness to 
common masses about this provision. 
(Para 7.6)  
Rectification of Black Spots

Further, there is a need to prioritize black spots based on the severity of accidents,

The Ministry should promote and support women-centr ic transport services, such as

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
Assessment of Demands For Grants 2023-24 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The shortfall is mainly in the major scheme of the Ministry, the Flagship Scheme, 
Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD and in promotion and publicity, both domestic and 
overseas. The Ministry has launched the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 Scheme and identified 55 
destinations under the same and budgetary  cuts at this stage would delay the implementation 
of the scheme. Howeve r, the Ministry has submitted that the shortfall in allocation is not 
likely to impact any Scheme as the Ministry can ask for additional funds at RE stage, if 
required. Further, the major Schemes of the Ministry are on -going in nature and will 
continue during the financial year 2024-2025 also. Accordingly, any pending liability on any 
Scheme can be met from the budget of 2024 -2025. The Committee recommends that if the 
Ministry requires additional funds at the R.E. stage the Ministry of Finance should alloca te 
the same. 
(Para 7) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1              The comments of the Committee are noted. 
  
Focus Area of the Ministry for 2023-24 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee observes that the Ministry had projected a B.E. of Rs. 320 crores for 
promotion and publicity for both domestic and overseas. The actual B.E is only Rs. 242 
crores. Keeping in view that 2023 is being promoted as the Visit India Year and the 
promotional schemes drawn up by the Ministry, the Committee feels that the  allocated 
amount would not be sufficient for the purpose. 
 (Para 23) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The recommendation of the committee is noted. Ministry will seek additional fund at 
RE stage, if required. However, it will also depend upon approval of the Competent 
Authority on continuation of Overseas Publicity and Promotion Scheme for the period upto 
2025-26. At present, only inevitable  expenditure under this scheme is made with the 
approval of the Department of Expenditure on case to case basis. 
 

3 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee also observes that the Focus areas of the Ministry for 2023 -24 are 
identical to the Focus areas in the year 2022 -23. The Committee notes that Focus Areas are 
defined in a budget to ensure that maximum effort and funds are provided to that area during 
that financial year to ensure success of the project. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry instead of routinely focusing on the same goals may set up precise achievable 
targets in the various areas of functioning. 
 (Para 27) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      The recommendation of the Committee is noted. 
  
 Monitoring of Projects Under Swadesh Darshan  
Recommendation/Observation 
4.        The Committee observes that in every year from 2019 onwards, the allocation  under 
the Scheme has been reduced by about 50% at the Revised Estimates stage. There is a 
marked decrease in utilisation of the allocated budget since 2019 onwards. The Committee 
notes that the Ministry has submitted that its Schemes being ongoing in natu re, any 
shortcomings in funds would be adjusted in the next Financial Year. The Committee notes 
that reduction at R.E. stage usually happens due to inefficient planning and implementations 
on the part of the Ministry. The Committee recommends that the Mini stry should re-examine 
its planning, organising and implementing strategy with a view to remove bottlenecks and 
inefficiencies at all levels. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should make all 
efforts for full utilization of funds under this scheme  so that the allocation is not reduced at 
R.E. stage. 
 (Para 40) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      Recommendation of the committee is noted. 
  
Swadesh Darshan 2.0 
Recommendation/Observation 
5.        The Committee observes that the Swadesh Darshan Scheme 1.0 had fifteen thematic 
circuits pertaining to culture, heritage, Eco -tourism, Wildlife, Rural, Cruises etc and almost 
all these themes have been repeated in the Scheme 2.0. With the exception of MICE and 
Wellness Tourism, no new areas for tourism have been i dentified. Consequent to the 
pandemic, staycations and working holidays have become popular tourism trends. Niche 
tourism areas like Caravan tourism, Gastronomy tourism, Avi tourism and Military tourism 
are gaining popularity. However, Scheme 2.0 has not e xplored these emerging trends in 
tourism.         

4 
 
(Para 46) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1      In Swadesh Darshan (1.0) scheme, projects were sanctioned under identified thematic 
circuits whereas objective of Swadesh Darshan 2.0, is to develop   responsible 
and  sustainable  tourism  destinations  following  a  tourist  and  destination  centric  approa
ch.  
  
5.2      As per the guidelines of the Swadesh Darshan 2.0, the Scheme will encourage 
development of benchmarks and standards for generic and theme specific development of 
tourism destinations and the States will follow the benchmarks and standards while planning 
and developing the projects. While major themes such as Culture and Heritage, Adventure 
Tourism, Eco Tourism, Wellness Tourism, MICE Tourism, Rural Tourism, Beach Tourism 
and Cruises (Ocean & Island) have been identified on the sch eme guidelines, all other 
themes will fall in one of the above major themes.    
  
5.3      The observation of the Committee is duly noted and it is submitted that the Ministry 
will continually strive to ensure that new and emerging niche areas of tourism a re not left out 
from the purview of its schemes.  
  
Recommendation/Observation 
6.        The Committee observes that major changes have been made in the funding pattern, 
disbursal of funds and receipt of Utilisation Certificates in the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 Scheme. 
New features of Impact Assessment of the projects under the Scheme and monitoring of the 
Scheme through a Comprehensive Portal by authorities at all levels have been introduced. 
The Committee appreciates the inclusion of these new features and feel s that impact 
assessment of tourist footfalls, employment generation at the ground level would help the 
Ministry in successful planning of future schemes. Digitization of all the processes of the 
Scheme and monitoring by Centre, State and District level authorities through a portal would 
assist the Ministry in management and reduce the delays. 
 (Para 48) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1      Observation of the Committee is noted. The unified portal for e -Services is being 
developed by the Ministry of Tourism. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
7.        The Committee has been informed that the Ministry has empanelled 10 Consultants for 
the SD 2.0 Scheme and has done three workshops with them regarding the vision, scope and 
deliverables of the Scheme. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry, drawing from 

5 
 
its experience in the previous Scheme, has endeavored to enhance the capability of the 
Consultants. 
 (Para 49) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1      Observation of the Committee is noted. 
  
 Impact of PRASHAD scheme 
Recommendation/Observation 
8.        The Committee observes that there are a total of 45 sanctioned projects under this 
scheme out of which only 20 have been completed. 9 projects under this Scheme are still 
pending completion with only upto 60% progress. There are still 16 projects yet to be 
developed under this scheme. Considering the fact that this scheme was initiated in 2014 -15 
the progress is very slow. The Committee observes that all the projects, both completed and 
ongoing, under PRASHAD have had de lays of at least one year (ANNEXURE -V). Some 
projects like the Development of Mathura -Vrindavan, U.P as Mega Tourist Circuit (Ph -II) 
and Development of Basic facilities at Vishnupad temple, Gaya, Bihar have had delay of 4 
years. The Committee also observes that some of the Targets in the EFC proposal of October 
2021 pertaining to this Scheme have not been achieved. 
 (Para 56) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1      The suggestion of the committee is noted. The Ministry of Tourism is regularly 
reviewing progress of the ongoing projects under the chairmanship of Secretary (Tourism). 
  
Promotion and Publicity  
Recommendation/Observation 
9.        The Committee notes that domestic tourism has been given special importance in the 
budget by schemes like “Dekho Apna Desh”, development of 50 new locations as tourist 
friendly destinations, the development of Vibrant Villages schemes in Border areas and 
establishment of Unity Malls. The Committee also notes that the Outcome Budget of the 
Ministry for the year 2023-24 has a target of 5% increase in domestic tourism. 
 (Para 74) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1      The observation of the Committee is noted. 
  
 
 

6 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10.        The Committee recommends that the Ministry may make efforts to utilise the budget 
effectively and then approach the Ministry of Finance for increased allocation at the Revised 
Estimates stage. 
 (Para 77) 
 Reply of the Ministry 
10.1      The recommendation of the Committee is noted. 
  
Human Resources Development 
Recommendation/Observation 
11.        The Committee acknowledges that the Hospitality Sector is the most affected sector 
in the Covid pandemic with massive revenue losses and job vulnerability still continuing to 
this day. However, the Committee notes that even in the pre-covid era, the number of persons 
placed after skill training is very low. The outcome of the skill training does not seem 
commensurate with the expenditure incurred on the programmes. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should review the quality of the programmes and faculty to 
enhance the skills of the students to an employable level. Pre -placement assistance such as 
mock interviews sessions may also be given to the students to help them in the job market 
(Para 95) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1      The recommendation of the Parliament Standing Committee has been well taken and 
the Division has already overhauled the program, right from the process of empanelment to 
bringing improvement in the Guidelines. The suggestion of P arliament Standing Committee 
is also noted for compliance. 
  
Safety and Security in Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
12.      The Committee notes that Swadesh Darshan 2.0 Scheme is a destination and tourist 
centric scheme. The foremost attribute in the i mage of a tourist destination is that of a safe 
and secure place and out of all the requirements of a tourist, safety is paramount. In the last 
few decades, safety and security have become even more of a pressing concern. The 
Committee is pleased to see th e initiatives taken by the Ministry to take up the matter of 
selecting 25 tourist sites as pilot project for formation of a separate police unit in the 
States/UTs. However, only 14 States have till date, deployed tourist police in one form or the 
other. The Committee exhorts the Ministry to continue to take up the matter with other states 
for creation and deployment of tourist police at destinations in their areas. 
(Para 103) 

7 
 
Reply of the Ministry         
12.1    Recommendation of the Committee is noted. The matter has been taken up with all the 
Principal Secretaries of the Tourism Department of the State Govt. and UT Admin reiterating 
the need to develop a uniform Tourist Police in all States and Union Territories. 
  
Utilisation Certificates 
Recommendation/Observation 
13.      The Committee observes from the details given by the Ministry that a number of 
Utilisation Certificate are pending to the tune of a cumulative amount of Rs. 370.45 crores. 
The Ministry has not indicated the year from which the UCs are pending. Since conditionality 
regarding submission of Utilization Certificates is a bar for the release of funds, the 
pendency of Utilization Certificates and the amount involved therein have implications for 
the further release of funds and  impinges on the effective implementation of tourism 
infrastructure projects formulated by the Ministry. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may take all efforts to reduce the pendency of the UCs. 
(Para 135) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1    The Ministry of Tourism notes the recommendation of the Committee. The Ministry 
of Tourism is undertaking regular review meetings with the implementing agencies on 
multiple issues including timely utilization of funds and submission of UCs. 
  
Niche Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
14.      The Committee observes that the pandemic has changed not only the way we live and 
work but also the way we travel. One of the major outcomes of the pandemic was the 
normalization of remote working which has given rise to the growing popularity of 
staycations, vacations in places near nature and remote places etc. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may take steps to conduct frequent market surveys and collect 
data to understand travel trends. The Committee observes that  data and market intelligence 
surveys are vital for creating a road map for the travel industry as future travel is going to be

2.        The Committee further finds that the entire budget allocation of Rs. 2400 crores is 
under Revenue Head with nil allocation to Capi tal Head. The Ministry has submitted that a 
major portion of the outlay amounting to Rs.1742 crores is earmarked for development of 
infrastructure for tourism development and Rs. 242.00 crores for promotion and branding 
activities. For tourism infrastructu re Schemes, an amount of Rs, 1412.00 crores is allocated 
for Swadesh Darshan, Rs. 250.00 crores is kept for the Scheme of PRASHAD (Pilgrimage 
Rejuvenation and Spiritual and Heritage Augmentation Drive) and Rs 80 crores is allocated 
for Scheme for Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development. 
(Para 17) 
3.        Much of the budgetary outlay is for development of infrastructure. Swadesh Darshan, 
the flagship scheme of the Ministry is focused on development of theme based infrastructur e. 
Infrastructure for all tourist amenities like creation of tourist information centre, reception 
centre, convention centres, cafeterias, beautification of tourist attractions are covered under 
this scheme. The Committee does not find it rational that tho ugh Capital assets are being 
created under the schemes of the Ministry, the entire expenditure is classified under Revenue. 
Revenue expenditure is short -term, recurring expenditure mostly pertaining to salaries, 
operating expenses, administrative costs etc . Due to its very nature, revenue expenditure 
cannot be reduced as the expenses such as salaries and wages are incurred irrespective of 
the activities carried out. The Committee finds however that for the last five years, the 
budgetary allocation of the Ministry has been halved at the Revised Estimates stage and even 

28 
 
this budget has remained unutilized. The Actual expenditure for the past five years has been 
much less than the budget allocated in Revised Estimates. 
(Para 18) 
4.        The Committee notes the submissions of the Ministry that though at the macro level, 
the budget is under Revenue Head, yet within the Schemes, there would be Object Heads 
pertaining to “Creation of Capital assets.” Under the two Major schemes, Swadesh Darshan 
and PRASHAD, ther e is no recurring expenditure on salary etc. These schemes are mainly 
meant for asset creation and only 5% funds are given for O&M (Operations and 
Maintenance). However, though only assets are being created under these schemes, the outgo 
of funds can be re duced depending on the progress of the projects and receipt of 
Utilization Certificates. 
(Para 19) 
5.        The Committee observes that creation of capital assets leads to value creation and 
generates future cash flows for the economy. Further, the multip lier effect of Capital 
expenditure is much more than that of the Revenue expenditure. In India, the multiplier effect 
of Capital expenditure made by the Central Government is estimated at 2.45 and for State 
Governments, it is around 2 while the multiplier effect of Revenue expenditure is only 0.99 
(RBI Bulletin, December, 2020) . Wrong classification therefore may not give the correct 
picture on total investment in infrastructure and may impact both the Index of Industrial 
Production and the GDP. The Committee notes that the classification as Revenue is arbitrary 
without following any valid criteria in case of various projects of Ministry of Tourism. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance 
and submit a detailed explanation to the Committee. 
(Para 20) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1      In compliance of the direction of the Hon‟ble Committee, the issue of classification of 
the entire allocation under revenue Head, has been examined thoroughly. The Ministry of 
Finance vide OM No.2(16) -B(P&A)/2022 dated 29.12.2022 conveyed the   allocation of 
funds to Ministry of Tourism wherein the entire allocation is under Revenue category.   The 
allocation is divided into two categories i.e. Scheme and Non -Scheme.  The allocation under 
the segment Scheme is used for implementation of various Schemes of the Ministry while 
the allocation under Non -Scheme is used for establishment expenses of the Ministry and its 
Regional Offices and subordinate office and the expenditure on IT ini tiatives.  The 
establishment expenditure includes, salaries, office expenses, rent and other items of 
expenditure.  Out of the allocation of Rs. 2,400.00 Crores for the financial year 2023 -2024, 
the allocation for Schemes is Rs. 2291.49 crores and Rs.108.51 crores is for Non-Scheme. 
5.2      As per the notification of Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure, forwarded 
vide OM dated 12 th December 2022, the entire allocation for different Schemes of the 
Ministry of Tourism amounting to Rs. 2291.49 cror es comes under Revenue 
Expenditure.  This includes Grants – in - Aid for creation of Capital Assets also.    The 
scheme of Swadesh Darshan, PRASHAD, Assistance to Central Agencies and Assistance to 

29 
 
IHM/FCI etc. evolve Grants in Aid for creation of Capital A ssets.  For the Schemes 
involving creation of infrastructure, funds are released under “Grants -in-Aid for Creation of 
Capital Assets”.   The infrastructure created under grants from the Ministry of Tourism is 
owned by the respective State Governments/autonomous bodies/Central Agencies.  Since the 
Ministry is giving Grants in Aid to the State Governments/Autonomous Bodies/Central 
Agencies for implementation of these Schemes, the ownership of the assets created is not 
with the Ministry.  The Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic 
Affairs‟s  OM No. F3/27/2014 -FRBM dated 9 th September 2014 clarified the Grants for 
Creation of Capital Assets  as under: 
5.3      Grants for creation of capital assets as a concept was introduced in the FRBM Act 
through the amendment in 2012.   The Act define grants for creation of capital assets as 
grants-in-aid given by the Central Government to state governments, autonomous bodies, 
local bodies and other scheme implementing agencies for creation of capital assets which are 
owned by these entities.  These grants are relevant for the projection of the effective revenue 
deficit, which has been defined under the Act as the difference between revenue deficit as 
defined under the Act and grants for creation of capital assets………” 
5.4      Out of the Non -Scheme components, as per the classification issued by Ministry of 
Finance as mentioned above, the components of ICT equipment like computers, laptops, etc., 
Machinery & Equipment and Furniture and Fixtures with cost exceeding Rs. 1 lakh or three 
years‟ of effective life and Motor Vehicles, fall under capital expenditure.   Under the Non -
Scheme segment, out of the allocation of Rs. 108.51 Crores, the total allocation for all the 
components mentioned above together comes  to Rs. 1.66 Crore.   The Ministry of Tourism 
had to open 58 New Heads of Accounts for the financial year 2023 -2024 at short notice due 
to creation of a number of New Heads by MoF.   In the process of opening so many new 
Heads and considering that these comp onents fall under Non -Scheme segment, the Head of 
Account for the above components was  also opened under Revenue Expenditure 
inadvertently. The Ministry will take action to open Heads of Accounts under Capital Section 
for these components.

The Government of Madhya Pradesh has come up with its proposal on  Safe Tourist 
Destination for Women in Madhya Pradesh,  the details of which are given below for 
reference:- 
16.1.1. Background  
Women should feel safe and most comfortable while travelling and enjoying tourist 
destinations.  This feeling and mindset is of utmost importance to boost the confidence and 
moral strength of women.     The fear of crime against women in tourist destinations affects 
women travellers restricting their travel to tourist destinations independently.   Women 
particularly either travelling solo or in a group, feel unsafe after dark due to feeble presence 
of women workforce in and around the touri st destinations, unavailability of public toilets, 

37 
 
lack of street lighting, public spaces like parks, temples, market areas, lack of information 
and support services for women add up to the situation.   A single event of violence against 
women is enough to deepen this perception and fear of violence.   All this limits the basic 
right and freedom of women as equal citizens to enjoy the world around them.  
  
16.1.2. Statistics  
The National crime records bureau statistics for 2014 in India show that a total of 3,37,922 
cases of crime against women were recorded as compared to 3,09,546 case in 2013 
indicating a rise of 9.2% in reporting of such crimes. The total number of registered rape 
cases is 36,735 (9% higher than the previous year).   Delhi UT has reported the highest crime 
rate (169.1) compared to 56.3 at all India level during the year 2014, followed by 
Assam(123.4), Rajasthan(91.4), Tripura(88.0), West Bengal(85.4), Madhya Pradesh (79.0) 
and Telangana(78.3)  
16.1.3. Objectives of Madhya Pradesh Tourism Boa rd for Safe and secure environment for 
women 
 Provide safe, secure and women friendly environment in and around tourist 
destinations. 
 Enhance women‟s confidence and desire to visit tourist destinations without any fear 
of violence and safety. 
 Development of women friendly spatial design, implementation and maintenance of 
infrastructural gaps. 
 Provide information and advisories about available resources and timely support 
services using technology. 
 Provide self defence training to women and girls.

skill enhancement programmes.

activities in tourist destination. 
 Promote community participation and awareness on women safety. 
 Formation of legal bodies and federations to organise local community intended for 
safety of women. 
 Strengthening the concept of “Atithi Devo Bhava” to build the belief of safety among 
all women tourists visiting the State.

exports duty credit scrips in the range of 5% to 7% of the net foreign exchange  earned

Development of Greenfield and Brownfield Airports and the Challenges thereof 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee notes that the Airports Authority of India (AAI) has emb arked upon a 
capital expenditure plan of Rs. 25,000 crores during the period 2019 -2024 for the 
development/ upgradation/ modernization of various airports in the country. This is a 
welcome move to improve the existing airport infrastructure in order to cat er to the ever - 
growing air traffic demand. The Committee recommends that the Ministry/AAI may ensure 
that traffic projections of the long -term future are factored in the planning and execution of 
these projects.  
 (Para 12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      Noted. 
  
Challenges Faced in Co-ordination between different Agencies and Departments  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may work with all the 
stakeholders to prescribe target deadlines, where possible,  which may be scrupulously 
followed to ensure smooth progress of airport projects.  
(Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      Noted. Projects are already being monitored at the highest level in the Ministry as also 
through various forums/portals such as Pro ject Monitoring Group (PMG), PRAGATI, and 
National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP), OCMS (Online Computerised Monitoring System) 
etc.  
  
Financing of Airport Projects and Foreign Direct Investment in Civil Aviation Sector  
Recommendation/Observation

Policy, 2020 issued by Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT),

 (Para 51) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      Matter of Fact.

4.        The Committee notes the details of the planned or proposed projects under the MAFI 
project of the IAF at 20 Civil Enclaves in the country. It notes that as per the details of Radio 
Navigational Aids (RNAs) which have been replaced or planned to be replaced under project 
MAFI at the Civil Enclaves as on 1st October, 2022, are as follows:- 
• RNAs replaced: 26  
• RNAs planned to be replaced: 23

4.1      Matter of record.

airports catering to fast growing civilian traffic hubs. The Committee appreciat es that both 
the Ministries of Civil Aviation and Defence have developed mechanism such as the „Land

airports, which is brought out by the fact that out of a total of 353 units deployed by CISF, 66 
units or 18.7 % is deployed at the airports only. The Committee also notes that the 
responsibility of the CISF to provide security is spread across a wide spectrum of 
establishments, as it provides security to 353 installations across the country including 
airports. It is also aware that the Civil Aviation Sector has seen an exponential growth and  is 
expected to grow at a faster pace in near future, which will enhance the need for manpower 
engaged in providing security for airports. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation may examine the feasibility of setting up a specialized security

 (Para 82) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1      At present ASG/ CISF is deployed at 66 airports in the country. Recommendations of

(Para 86)

7.1      Recommendation of the Committee is noted.

Green and sustainable initiatives at airports and civil enclaves

 CHAPTER-II 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
  
Development of Greenfield and Brownfield Airports and the Challenges thereof 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that the Government has granted in-principle approval for 21 
Greenfield Airport projects since 2008, which is a crucial step towards meeting the growing 
air traffic demand in the country. However, more Greenfield airports need to be developed to 
cater to the increasing demand and to achieve the vision laid out in the National Civil 
Aviation Policy, 2016 to enab le 30 crore domestic ticketing by 2022 and 50 crore by 2027. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should encourage more State 
Governments and private airport developers to propose Greenfield airport projects and to 
streamline its approval process to expedite the development of airports. 
 (Para 11) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      Government of India (GoI) has formulated a Greenfield Airports (GFA) Policy, 2008 
for development of Greenfield airports in the country. As per the policy, if any d eveloper 
including the State Government desires to develop an airport, they are required to identify a 
suitable site and get the Pre-feasibility Study conducted for construction of airport and submit 
a proposal to the Central Government for 'Site Clearance' followed by 'In-Principle' approval.  
1.2      As per the request of Project Proponent(s), Airports Authority of India also assists and 
prepares Pre-feasibility Report, OLS Report, DPR etc. relating to development of Greenfield 
Airport. 
1.3      As on da te, under GFA Policy, 2008, 12 Greenfield airports viz. Durgapur in West 
Bengal, Shirdi and Sindhudurg in Maharashtra, Kannur in Kerala, Pakyong in Sikkim, 
Kalaburagi and Shivamogga in Karnataka, Orvakal (Kurnool) in Andhra Pradesh, Kushinagar 
in Uttar Pra desh, Itanagar in Arunachal Pradesh, Mopa in Goa and Rajkot in Gujarat have 
been operationalized. Further, Six more Greenfield Airports, viz. Noida(Jewar) in Uttar 
Pradesh, Navi Mumbai in Maharashtra, Vijayapura and Hassan in Karnataka, Dholera in 
Gujarat and Bhogapuram in Andhra Pradesh are under various stages of development.  
1.4      Further, Site Clearance for setting up Greenfield Airports at Mandi, Kottayam and Puri 
have recently been accorded. Moreover, applications for setting up Greenfield airport s at 
Doloo(Silchar), Kota and Raichur are under examination. 
  
  
  

10 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee observes that the list of airports under planning or expansion includes 
several airports that are being developed under PPP mode. PPPs can  bring in private sector 
expertise and investment, which can help in accelerating the airport development process 
and improving operational efficiency. Therefore, the government should encourage more 
PPPs for airport development, especially for Greenfield airports. 
 (Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The Ministry agrees with the recommendations of the Committee and has encouraged 
development of new Airports by State Governments and Private partners. It can be seen that 
out of 21 'in principle'  approval granted by MoCA for setting up of 21 Greenfield airports 
across the country, Projects like Durgapur, Sindhudurg, Kannur, Mopa have been 
operationalized with Private investment or under PPP. Other Greenfield airports under 
development viz., Navi Mumbai, Noida (Jewar), Bhogapuram are also being executed under 
PPP mode. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee desires to know the number of airports with throughput above 1.5 
mppa which have an ASQ rating of less than 4.5 and number of airports with throughput less 
than 1.5 mppa which have an ASQ rating of less than 4.0 as on date. The Committee may be 
apprised of the steps being taken by AAI to upgrade the quality of services provided at each 
such airport with low ASQ ratings.  
(Para 17) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      The ASQ survey is conducted exclusively for Major airports. In India, the airports 
Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA) designates major airports based on their passenger 
footfall. Previously, major airports were classified as those with an annual  passenger count of 
1.5 million. However, this threshold has now been raised to 3.5 million passengers annually. 
Consequently, the ASQ survey is carried out for airports with a footfall exceeding 3.5 million 
passengers per annum. Airport Operators are comm itted to provide high -quality services to 
passengers and continuously improving their airport experiences.At present, the ASQ survey 
has been conducted at 13 AAI airports with a throughput of 3.5 million passengers per annum 
or more. All of these airports,  except Srinagar, received ASQ ratings above 4.5. Srinagar 
airport received a rating of 4.3. 
3.2      The primary issue leading to a lower rating at Srinagar airport was the long waiting 
time at the Drop Gate due to limited X -ray machines and check points by CRPF. To address 
this, AAI has taken the following steps:- 
 Installed additional 4 X-BIS machines for security screening. 
 Widened the road at the Drop Gate to reduce check-in times. 

11 
 
 Introduced 14 E -carts for passenger transportation between the Drop Gate  and the 
airport, significantly enhancing convenience.

39 
 
in order to achieve the desired growth rate in the aviation sector in the country. The

2.1      Government of India has permitted 100% Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in 
Greenfield and Brownfield airport projects under the FDI Policy. Further, Government of 
India has made several efforts in the form of policy decisions which inter -alia include

Land Value Capture Mechanism  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee notes that land acquisition is one of the biggest expenditures incurred 
on the development of an airport. Given the consistently rising land acquisition costs for 
public infrastructure projects,  the present sources for financing of the same i.e., budgetary 
allocation of the Ministry, Public -Private-Partnership and AAI revenue, might not be 
sufficient. The Committee feels that the Value Capture Mechanism can augment the financial 
requirements of t he airport sector in the country. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may conduct a detailed analysis of the possible implementation of the Value Capture 
Mechanism to generate revenue for investment in further development, maintenance and 
expansion of airports across the country.  
 (Para 55) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      As per the provisions of National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP 2016), State Govt. are 
required to provide the requisite land for airport development and expansion on free of cost 
basis to AAI. The State gets benefitted by the economic development i n the area of influence 
of airport project and increase in value of land.  
3.2      Land being State subject, the benefits are transferred to State Govt. for increase in 
circle rates, stamp duty and other economic activities in surrounding areas. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
3.3      The Committee desires to know the comments of the Ministry on the ‘Land Value 
Capture Mechanism’ to augment the financial requirements of airport sector in the 
country and reiterates that the Ministry may conduct a det ailed analysis of the possible 
implementation of the Value Capture Mechanism to generate revenue for investment in 
further development, maintenance and expansion of airports across the country.

Recommendation/Observation

 (Para 180)

take up major technical repairs as well. Aircraft manufacturers (OEMs) may be encouraged 
to open MRO facilities in India.  
 (Para 181) 
13.      The Committee also observes that most of the foreign Aircraft Manufacturers & OEMs 
prefer to utilize their own MROs established abroad despite reduced labour, shipping,

recommends that the Ministry may focus on highlighting these aspects to prospec tive MROs 
who want to set up establishments in the country. The Committee is of the view that the 
growth of the MRO sector will also depend on how efficiently it can address and remove the 
key challenges faced by MRO players in India. It hopes that the Min istry will make all out 
efforts to implement the various fiscal measures at the ground level and also ensure proactive 
interaction with MRO industry to remove any bottlenecks that may arise.  
 (Para 182) 
14.      The Committee is of the opinion that since MRO services constitute a significant 
portion of overall expenditure of any airlines operator, setting up MRO services in the 
country would reduce the expenditure on MRO services and subsequently reduce the airfares 
in the domestic routes, which will conse quently reduce the cost of air travel and benefit the 
passengers.  
 (Para 183) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1    There are 150 (Operator + Standalone) AMOs/Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul 
MROs approved in India for Line/Base maintenance. Out of which 49 standal one MROs 
approved for base maintenance and 07 are capable to carrying out the maintenance and 
overhaul of aircraft and components. 

46 
 
14.2    Government seeks to facilitate setting up of aircraft MRO services in India through 
various policy, regulatory and ot her incentives and the Government has taken various 
measures to create a conducive environment for the development of Aircraft Maintenance, 
Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services. 
14.3    With a view to incentivise the growth of MROs in the country and also co ntribute to 
the ease of doing business, MoCA has brought out the new MRO Guidelines in Sept. 2021 
with a view to create a congenial atmosphere in the country for the development of the MRO 
industry for aircraft/ helicopter/ drones and their engines and oth er parts. These guidelines 
inter-alia provide for transparency in the allotment of land doing away with levy of any 
royalty or cess of whatsoever nature on MRO operators and at AAI airports through call of 
open tenders. 
14.4    Further on 9th June 2023, AA I has issued Land Management Circular through which 
allotment of land/ space for setting up MROs (for self/3rd party) at AAI Airports to willing 
agencies on card rate basis for a period of 25 years. No royalty/ concession fee shall be 
payable/ applicable for self and 3rd party MRO services. 
14.5    The other key measures taken by the Government to incentivise MROs in the country 
are:- 
i. GST on MRO has been reduced from 18% to 5% with full Input Tax Credit from 1st 
April, 2020. 
ii. Transactions sub -contracted by f oreign original equipment manufacturers (OEMs)/ 
MRO to domestic MRO are treated as 'exports' with zero -rated GST from 1st April, 
2020 
iii. Exempted Customs Duty on tools and tool kits 
iv. Reduced Goods and Services Tax rates on various spare parts, accessories, and  
consumables 
v. Simplified clearance processing of parts 
vi. Relaxed restriction on utilization of duty-free parts from one year to three years 
vii. Extended stay in India of foreign aircraft for entire duration of MRO work or 6 
months, whichever is lesser 
viii. Revised the Notification to enable export of serviceable parts 
ix. 100% Foreign Direct Investment permitted via automatic route for MRO 
x. Liberalized policy for borrowing and lending in Foreign Currency and Rupees on 
competitive terms for MROs 
xi. Modalities prescribed for con cessional temporary imports of spare parts by foreign 
airlines for repair of their aircraft in transit. 
14.6    The taxation issues pertaining to MRO sector have also been taken up with Ministry of 
Finance in the meetings held between M/o Civil Aviation an d M/o Finance, as well as vide 
follow-up letters. Most recently, a meeting was held between Hon'ble Minister of Civil 

47 
 
Aviation and Hon'ble Finance Minister on 26/06/2023 wherein the taxation issues pertaining 
to civil aviation sector, including MRO sector, were reiterated. 
14.7    Some of the positive developments in the MRO sector to promote investment and tie -
ups regarding airframe, engine and component in the  country  are as follows: 
 Airbus and Boeing have signed collaboration agreements with GMR and Ai r Works 
respectively in February 2021 
 Pratt & Whitney has started aircraft engine repairs in association with Air India 
Engineering Services Limited (AIESL). 
 General electric (GE) established an engine / overhaul repair facility at Nagpur, the 
first phase of engine MRO is operational and till date quick turn repairs of engines has 
been carried at Nagpur engine test cell preparatory area. 
 Several rounds of discussions have been held with the representatives of Safran at 
various levels regarding the proposed MRO facilities in India. Safran has committed 
to invest USD 150 million for setting up an aircraft engine MRO at Hyderabad. The 
proposed timeline is 31st December, 2024. 
 M/s Boeing have: (a) Constructed a state-of-the-art C-17 facility, which could be used 
for civil MRO as well, (b) Operationalized P -8I defence MRO in India, (c) 
Announced with Spirit a component parts MRO in February 2023, (d) Announced a 
737-cargo conversion line in March 2023 and (e) Partnering with Safran on the engine 
MRO it is building for the 737 by 2025. 
 PHL is already in talks with Russian OEMs to jointly set up MRO facilities in India 
for Russian origin Helicopters in Civil/Defence market. 
 HAL has aligned itself to achieve objectives of MoCA to make India a Global MRO 
hub. Various M RO services are planned at HAL Nasik for narrow body and general 
aviation aircraft.  In this regard HAL is collaborating with OEMs as well as Global 
MRO players. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation

development of Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) facilities in the Country.

especially in the North-Eastern Region, Hilly Areas and Islands including Lakshadweep

1. Energy Conservation Initiatives:To optimize energy consumption, AAI has 
replaced conventional light fixtures with energy-efficient LED fittings, old equipment 
with star rated energy efficient equipments, installed occupancy/motion sensors, 
adopted highest GRIHA-rated standards for construction of new terminals, use of 
automatic sliding doors and air-curtains to minimise air-conditioning losses and

air-conditioning and other electrical systems.

in enhancement of ground operational efficiency by encouraging intersection 
departures.

operations has resulted in improvement of on-time performance of airlines, thereby 
reducing departure congestion and queuing of aircrafts. 
3. No of boarding gates, X-ray machines and Check-in counters are being augmented to 
improve the operational efficiency of airports.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Airfare Regulations in the Past  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes the Airfare regulations that existed in the past and observes that 
the Air Corporations Act, 1953 required the various airline corporations to seek approval of 
Central Government for fixing airfares. Thereafter, on 21 st March, 1994, the said Act was 
repealed and the Indian Domestic Aviation Sector was totally deregulated and the airlines 
had the freedom to fix airfares. 
 (Para 4) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes that as per the airfare regulations existing earlier, the airfares 
were fully regulated by the Government which had put in place a mechanism to keep airfares 
under check. Thereafter, deregulation of airfares effectively came into effect from 21st March, 
1994 with the repeal of the Air Corporation Act, 1953 and the various airlines were free to 
fix airfares. 
(Para 5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937  
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee notes the amendment in Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 on 16 th 
April, 2009, which presently forms the basis of the legislation for airfare regulations. It also 
notes that as per the Rule 135(1), the airlines shall establish tariff, keeping in mind factors 
such as reasonable profit besides cost of operation, character istics of service and generally 
prevailing tariff, to rationalise airfares despite its deregulation, consequent upon repeal of 
Air Corporations Act, 1953. 
 (Para 8) 
 

3 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee also observes that Rule 135(2) requires the publication of the tariff by 
the airlines on its website/ daily newspapers or displaying it conspicuously in their office/ or 
the agent‟s office. Further, Section 135(2A) requires the airlines to sh ow the total amount 
payable by the passenger including the breakup such as taxes, fees for services/ facilities or 
other charges, which should be mentioned in the passenger ticket vide Rule 135 (2B). 
 (Para 9) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee notes another significant requirement in Rule 135(3), wherein every 
airline is required to maintain all records relating to tariff and the requirement to produce 
such records to Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) for inspection. The Committee 
observes that the aforesaid Rule provides for supervision and inspection of DGCA (Ministry 
of Civil Aviation) on air tariffs being fixed by the airlines. 
(Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. Rule 135 (4) also empowers the DGCA to issue directions to airlines, if it is satisfied 
that the airlines have charged excessive/ predatory airfares or indulged in oligopolistic 
practice. Further, as per Rule 135 (5), the aforesaid directions of DGCA have to be compiled 
with by the airline concerned. 
 (Para 11) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 Observation has been Noted.

Power of DGCA to Regulate Tariffs  
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee observes that DGCA has a Tariff Monitoring Unit that monitors 
airfares on certain routes at regular intervals to ensure that the airlines do not charge 
airfares outside a range declared by them. However, the DGCA does not have any power to 
regulate tariffs based on the data generated by the Tariff Monitoring Unit as the process of 
airfare regulation has been dispensed with, consequent upon the repeal of the Air 
Corporation Act, 1953. 
(Para 17) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee notes that presently airlines are free to charge reasonable airfares as 
per their operational viability subject to compliance of Rule 135(1) of the Aircraft Rules, 
1937. Besides, currently, there is no provision under which Government is required to 
monitor the seat booking fees of airlines and the airlines sell tickets as per their respective 
distribution system, which is as per the global practice. 
 (Para 25) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee also observes that most of the airlines except AI Express had 
accumulated losses from FY 2019 -20 to 2021 -22. The Committee is aware that the Civil 
Aviation Industry had suffered a major setback on account  of Covid-19 pandemic and needs 
to recover its losses and regain its pre-pandemic level and then grow at an even faster rate to 
realise its    set targets. As such, the Committee is of the opinion that a fine balance needs to 
be maintained so that the interests of the airlines as well as the passengers are kept in mind.  
(Para 26) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 The observation has been noted.

Reasonable Profit, Generally Prevailing Tariff and Mechanism followed for Fixing 
Airfares  
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Committee notes the replies of the representatives of various airlines as regards 
its query on the mechanism adopted by them to calculate the quantum of „reasonable profit‟. 
The airlines had commented that the prevailing air tariff on a particular  route is a result of 
demand-supply balance. Besides, airlines work on a „Cost Recovery Model‟, so as to recover 
all costs related to flight operations, rather than on a set target to achieve „reasonable 
profit‟. One of the airlines had also stated that th ey do not set a target „reasonable profit‟ 
and the practice of „Revenue Management‟ is followed which takes into account demand and 
supply. Representatives of an airline had also stated that pricing aspects depend on market 
situation and the ticket fares cannot be quantified in advance. 
 (Para 41) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. As regards, the Committee‟s query regarding the minimum number of tickets needed 
to be sold on a particular route for airlines to break -even, the airlines were of the opinion 
that since most of the airlines have been unprofitable for most parts of their existence, the 
airlines were not able to achieve break -even point. Hence, currently, no such system exists in 
India. Airline representatives opined that the number of tickets sold for break -even depends 
on demand-supply dynamics based on which Revenue Management System does the pricing. 
 (Para 42) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 The observation has been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
12. The Committee observes that though the concept of establishing tariffs on basis of 
„reasonable profit‟ is ingrained in the Rule 135(1) of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, yet none of the 
airlines has adopted a mechanism to calculate  the quantum of „reasonable profit‟. All the 
airlines are instead following the demand -supply dynamics through the „Revenue 
Management System‟ and hence, airfares are fixed accordingly. 
 (Para 43) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1 The observation has been noted.

Dynamic Pricing and Global Standards  
Recommendation/Observation

These models are based on forecasting and optimizat ion tools. It also observes that there are

17.1 Observation of the Committee.

CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Power of DGCA to Regulate Tariffs  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee took exception to the Ministry‟s concluding remarks during the  
presentation and during their deposition in the meeting of the Committee held on 8 th May, 
2023, and their written replies that regulation of airfare is not desirable for the overall 
growth of the aviation sector. The Committee reiterates its view that passengers should 
receive a fair deal at all times and recommends that the Ministry shou ld have a relook in its 
policy regarding regulation of airfare tariff in view of the sudden surge in airfares in normal 
times as also during disasters and calamities and take appropriate actions in consonance 
with the powers delegated to it under Rule 135 of the Aircraft Act, 1937. 
 (Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Internationally civil aviation has a highly seasonal market. The Indian Market is also 
characterized by high (May to mid -July and October to mid -January) and low (mid July to 
September and mid -January to April) seasons. Traffic is usually high in the month s of May 
and June, thru mid -July the international traffic flows are high, thus contributing to the 
domestic feed as well. July through September is traditionally leaner period as travel is 
restricted due to monsoon and other religious reasons. In October,  with the festive season 
starting Dussehra, traffic picks up again and by middle of January the demand diminishes. 
Till about the last week of April, this trend of softening of demand continues and again, due 
to summer holidays, the demand increases.  
1.2 Passengers are extremely price-sensitive. Price is the primary driver to pick an airline 
especially for leisure travel. All airlines compete on price with other carriers in the respective 
markets. Airlines adopt dynamic pricing by changing prices often dep ending on the day of 
the week, time of day, and number of days before the flight factoring in different components 
such as, how many seats a flight has, departure time, and average cancellations on similar 
flights. Dynamic pricing plays a crucial role in d etermining how airlines recover its cost and 
improve their revenue per flight. 
1.3 DGCA operates a Tariff Monitoring Unit, which monitors airfares on select routes 
including operationally constrained routes and prepares a report on a monthly basis to ensur e 
that airlines do not charge airfares outside the fares declared by them and any abnormally 
high airfare on such sector was brought to the notice of the respective airline for their self -
regulation.  

11 
 
1.4 DGCA has been asked to examine the relevant CAR/Circular in respect of Sub Rule 2 
as the existing provision under Sub Rule 2 doesn‟t specify any frequency of publication of 
tariff. The period of 24 h ours is also to be examined to arrive at suitable time period to avoid 
frequent and last day changes in tariff, bringing any surge in airfare. 
1.5 Moreover, Government has adopted a proactive approach to address the concerns 
emerging from rising of airfares. Consultation s with airlines are carried out on regular basis 
and airlines are asked to exercise moderation in pricing and keep passengers interest in mind. 
1.6 Also, airlines have committed to ensure that airfares do not surge during events such 
as natural disasters, calamities, civil unrest, etc. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes that the Airports Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA) has a 
mandate to determine tariff for aeronautical services of Major Airports only, vide Section 
13(1) (a) of the AERA Act, 2008. Since the tariff for aeronautical services is one of the 
components for airfares , the Committee desires to know how airfare is determined across 
Airports even though aeronautical service charges are applicable only to Major airports. 
 (Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Aeronautical charges are applicable on all the airports. Tariff d etermination for 
aeronautical services provided by the airport operator for all the „major airports‟ across the 
country is being done by AERA. Aeronautical tariff for „non-major airports‟ is determined by 
Ministry of Civil Aviation. The aeronautical charges are one of the components of the air fare 
being collected by airlines from the passengers, which are applicable for all the airports. 
 
Global Data Analysis  
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee notes the analysis of the ACI, which highlights the progressive 
increase in airfares both in domestic and international routes both in Indian as well as in 
other international markets. The Committee also notes the concerns of the ACI on excessive 
airfares which in the long term would reduce the demand for a ir travel and have a 
detrimental effect on its future growth. 
(Para 49) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 ACI is a consortium of airports and not a government organization. The observation is 
based on the report of ACI which is n ot based on factual parameters. It is based on 
presumptions. The airfare is cyclic and seasonal and it varies from place to place. Moreover, 
it also depends on the financial/revenue management of the airlines. It is also to mention that 

12 
 
airlines deploy their available capacity on the basis of market demand, supply parameters and 
RBD. There are multiple players in the market. 
3.2 Further, reasonableness of airfares in India can be judged from the fact that airfares in 
India are much lower than those charged by airlines in most countries, for the same distance. 
3.3 There is no study showing any adverse impact of airfare on reduction in air travel. 
Rather, the domestic passenger traffic is showing an upward trend. As per traffic data 
published by DGCA, the passenger growth for the Month of August, 2023 is 22.81% 
compared to August, 2022. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee also notes ACI‟s advice to the Airlines to exercise fair pricing that 
supports recovery and safeguards consumers‟ interests. ACI also advises the airlines agains t 
exploiting the supply-demand imbalance at the expense of customers by restricting capacity. 
(Para 50) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 ACI is a consortium of airports and not a government organization. Airline industry 
functions on a cost recovery model. Airlines commit to operating flights long in advance 
without any assurance that revenues will cover costs. Airlines deploy all their available 
capacity on the basis of market demand, supply parameters with multi -players and RBD. In 
case airlines are not in  a position to recover their cost and marginal profit, they will not be 
able to invest in additional aircraft, staff or routes. Further, cost structure of airlines is under 
tremendous pressure, and on revenue front, there is very little scope to gain windf all profit by 
airlines. 
 
Analysis of Global Practice for Ticket Pricing  
Recommendation/Observation 
5. It is evident that as per the international practices, though IATA Recommended 
Practices (RPs) are non -binding, yet these are acknowledged by the various  international 
airlines as a guiding factor. However, each airline modifies it to suit their own commercial 
practices, subject to National laws which get priority over the IATA RPs. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may ensure the prop er implementation of the 
existing Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 which is the National Law in India for fixing of 
reasonable airfares by the airlines, for the benefit of the passengers. 
 (Para 73) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 DGCA is a safety regulator and has a Tariff Monitoring Unit that monitors airfares on 
certain routes on monthly basis and on sector specific basis on 52 sectors to ensure that the 
airlines do not change airfares outside a range declared by them. 

13 
 
5.2 DGCA being the safety regulator, ensures that the airlines publish their Tariff Sheet 
on their websites, in compliance to Rule 135 (2) of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, in order to bring 
transparency for the passengers.   DGCA also ensures that the airfares charged by airlines‟ as 
displayed on their websites are as per Sub Rule 2A i.e. the total amount payable by passenger 
along with a complete break -up of the total amount. Complete break -up of airfare is printed 
on passenger tickets as per sub -rule 2B. The above are checked on a daily basis and  airlines 
are in compliance of these Rules.  
5.3 DGCA has been directed to examine the relevant CAR/Circular i.r.o Sub Rule 2 as the 
existing provision under Sub Rule 2 doesn‟t specify any frequency of publication of tariff. 
The period of 24 hrs also to be  examined to arrive at suitable time period to avoid changes in 
tariff bringing surge in airfare 
5.4 The airlines maintain records of the airfares charged by them. In the last 10 years, all 
airlines have been in compliance to Rule 135(1) and (2) and hence,  no inspection of records 
(domestic or international carrier) relating to tariff established by an airline has been carried 
out by DGCA. 
5.5 Provisions of Sub -Rule 4 on predatory/ excessive pricing are primarily the remit of 
Competition Commission of India  (CCI). CCI carried out investigation regarding excessive 
airfares during periods of force -majeure conditions in year 2011. However, CCI in its order 
no. 01/2011 dated 11.01.2012 noted that there was no contravention of rules by airlines 
regarding airfares and fares are subject to market conditions of demand and supply  
5.6 Hon‟ble Delhi High Court in Federation of Indian Airlines Vs DGCA &  Anr. (2017) 
has also held that DGCA cannot determine the tariff for airlines or their products. In the 
judgement, Hon‟ ble High Court of Delhi ordered that DGCA cannot determine tariff for 
specified flight product and set aside the provision of “Check -in baggage charges” contained 
in Air Transport Circular 02 of 2016 titled “Unbundling of services and fees by scheduled 
airlines”. As per the order, it has been expressly provided that DGCA would not fix the fee 
for „unbundled services‟ as airfare is determined by market forces.

Impact of Airport Tariff on Airfares  
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee observes that there is a lot of variation in User Development Fees 
(UDF), for domestic passengers, ranging from Nil to Rs. 480 and for International 
passengers, from Rs. 52.56 to Rs. 1200. The Committee desires to know the reasons for the 
wide variation in UDF rates both for domestic and international passengers which is one of 
the components of airfares, leading to rise in airfares. 
 (Para 84) 
 
 

15 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Government of India has set up Airports Econ omic Regulatory Authority of India 
(AERA) under the AERA Act, 2008. AERA has a mandate to determine tariff for 
aeronautical services provided by Airport Operators at „Major Airports‟. 
7.2 AERA determines aeronautical charges of „Major Airports‟ such as Landing, Parking, 
UDF etc. considering the following factors:- 
(i) Return on Investment; 
(ii) Operating Expenditure; 
(iii) Depreciation; and 
(iv) Tax paid to the Government. 
7.3 For determination of airport tariffs, the Airport Operator submits the Multi Year 
Tariff Proposal (MYTP)/annual Tariff Proposal (ATP) to AERA.  AERA determines the

10.2 The airline pricing system runs in multiple levels (buckets) which are in line with 
practices being followed Globally. The prices are fixed by airlines keeping in mind the 
market, demand, seasonality and other market forces. The airfare increase s with increase in 
demand of seats as the lower fare buckets get sold out fast when bookings are offered by

18 
 
offered which would entail travelling even during peak seasons on low fares. The fare

Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee, therefore, observes that ever since the amendment made in Rule 135 
of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 in April, 2009, sufficient legislative safe guards have been made in 
the Aircraft Rules, 1937, to ensure that airfares are affordable and in case of any violation by 
the airlines, the Government can take action against the said airline regardless of the 
deregulation of the airfares, due to repeal of Air Corporation Act, 1953. The Committee calls 
upon the DGCA, Ministry of Civil Aviation to safeguard the interests of the air commuters by 
invoking the overriding powers vested on it in the Rules. 
 (Para 12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      Airlines are free to establish their airfares as per their operation viabilities. With the 
repeal of Air Corporations Act in March 1994, the Indian domestic aviation was totally 
deregulated. As per prevailing regulation, airfares are not regulated by the Government. 
1.2 The domestic airline pricing runs in multiple levels (bucket or RBD) which is in line 
with the practice followed globally. The lower fare in the fare bucket is available for advance 
booking much earlier. As time lapses and date of journey approaches clos er, the fare in 
higher side of fare bucket is made available as per the respective airline policy. The airfares 
remain affordable for air commuters booking much earlier from the date of departure. 
1.3 DGCA ensures that the airlines publish their Tariff Sheet on their websites, in 
compliance to Rule 135 (2) of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, in order to bring transparency for the 
passengers.  DGCA also ensures that the airfares charged by airlines as displayed on their 
websites are as per Sub Rule 2A, i.e., the  total amount payable by passenger along with a 
complete break-up of the total amount. Complete break -up of airfare is printed on passenger 
tickets as per sub-rule 2B. The above are checked on a daily basis by DGCA and airlines are 
found in compliance of these Rules. 
1.4 However, DGCA has been asked to examine the relevant CAR/Circular  in respect of 
Sub Rule 2 as the existing provision under Sub Rule 2 doesn‟t specify any frequency of 
publication of tariff. The period of 24 h ours is also to be examined to a rrive at suitable time 
period to avoid frequent and last day changes in tariff bringing any surge in airfare. 
1.5 The airlines maintain records of the airfares charged by them. In the last 10 years, all 
airlines have been in compliance to Rule 135(1) and ( 2) and hence, no inspection of records 
(domestic or international carrier) relating to tariff established by an airline has been carried 
out by DGCA. 

31 
 
1.6 Provisions of Sub-Rule 4 on predatory/ excessive pricing are primarily in the domain 
of Competition Co mmission of India (CCI). CCI carried out investigation regarding 
excessive airfares during periods of force -majeure conditions in year 2011. However, CCI in 
its order no. 01/2011 dated 11.01.2012 noted that there was no contravention of rules by 
airlines regarding airfares and fares are subject to market conditions of demand and supply.  
1.7 Moreover, Hon‟ble Delhi High Court in Federation of Indian Airlines Vs DGCA &  
Anr. (2017) has also held that DGCA cannot determine the tariff for airlines or their products. 
In the judgement, Hon‟ble High Court of Delhi ordered that DGCA cannot determine tariff 
for specified flight product and set aside the provision of “Check -in baggage charges” 
contained in Air Transport Circular 02 of 2016 titled “Unbundling of servic es and fees by 
scheduled airlines”. As per the order, it has been expressly provided that DGCA would not 
fix the fee for „unbundled services‟ as airfare is determined by market forces. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
1.8 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee notes that DGCA 
has not inspected the records of airlines over the last 10 years and without any 
inspection, it has stated that airlines have complied with the rules. Hence, it does not 
agree with the reply and reasons given  by the Ministry. The Committee opines that a 
case of violation by airlines can only be detected, in case the records are inspected by 
DGCA. While the Ministry mentions that fares are subject to market conditions of 
demand and supply, the Committee feels t hat this explanation might be exploited by 
airlines to justify excessive pricing during unforeseeable conditions. Further, while the 
Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry, it feels that the period of 24 
hours which needs to be examined to a rrive at suitable time period to avoid frequent 
and last day changes in tariff bringing any surge in airfare may be examined in 
consultation and implemented at the earliest.

Reasonable Profit, Generally Prevailing Tariff and Mechanism followed for Fixing 
Airfares  
Recommendation/Observation 
4.        The Committee notes that though the term „reasonable profit‟ is given under Rule 
135(1) of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, yet there i s no specific definition or Rule or any other 
guidelines to define it and these expressions are liable to be misunderstood, besides 
encouraging arbitrary actions. The Committee is of the opinion that the term „reasonable 
profit‟ should be clearly defined i n the Rules, taking into account various financial and 
operational factors, as it is the most significant aspect for controlling surge in airfares, 
which affects the common man. 
 (Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 

34 
 
4.1      With the repeal of The Air Corporation Act 1994, Airfares have been deregulated and 
are determined by market forces. During the consultation with airlines, it has emerged that 
„reasonable profit‟ is a part of airlines revenue management which is based on demand and 
supply model. Airlines globally work on a cost recovery model rather than on a set target to 
achieve reasonable profit. 
4.2 The reasonableness of tariff is a function of demand and supply, variations in demand 
by season, during the day of the week, time of day, directional ity, number of days before the 
flight, capacity deployed on the route, variations in cost of operations, etc. 
4.3 Reasonableness of airfares in India can be judged from the fact that airfares in India 
are much lower than those charged by airlines in most c ountries, for the same distance. 
Average airfares in India are also quite low.  While it is the core goal of every enterprise to 
maximise shareholder value, the fact remains that the Indian airline industry continues to face 
considerable financial distress. 
4.4 Reasonableness of pricing also needs to be viewed in the context of overall network 
profitability as airlines may also operate on loss making routes to generate network feeds.  
Revenue management enables airlines to stimulate demand by offering low far es to price -
sensitive travellers and higher airfares to price-insensitive corporate travellers. 
4.5 Few of major financial and operational factors relevant in determination of airfares 
are as follows:- 
 ATF Accounts for about 40% of the operational cost of airlines. ATF prices have 
experienced high volatility. ATF prices doubled within an year (Rs. 69,060/KL in 
July 2021 to 141,233/KL July 2022) and are still at Rs. 118,199/KL which is 171%  of 
July, 2021 price level. Airfares have not increased in same propo rtion with the 
increase in ATF prices.  
 Internationally civil aviation has a highly seasonal market. The Indian Market is also 
characterized by high (may to mid -July and October to mid -January) and low seasons 
(mid July to September and mid January to April). 
 The airline pricing is highly elastic. Pricing of air tickets by airlines is pegged against 
key competitors on the given route, keeping in view relative product strengths. 
 Indian aviation market is price competitive due to multiple players, seasonal ma rket 
depending on demand and supply.  
4.6 Keeping in mind the above factors, it is noted that: 
a. Cost structure of airlines is under tremendous pressure, and 
b. On revenue front, there is very little scope to gain windfall profit by airlines.  
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
4.7      The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry, but is still of the opinion that the
